#7809. What Actually Happens When Semi-Trucks Stop at Weigh Stations?

Those roadside scales do more than weigh semitrucks. Here’s what inspectors check and what happens when a truck pulls into a weigh station.

Drivers pass truck weigh stations all the time, but few know everything these stations do or what happens when a truck pulls in. Once a semitruck exits and rejoins the highway, it’s hard to tell what goes on in between.

Learn what happens when a truck pulls in, what inspectors look for, and why some drivers can keep going.

Truck weigh stations help states enforce weight limits and spot safety problems. Trucks can weigh too much overall or carry too much weight on certain axles, putting extra strain on roads and bridges. On the Interstate System, the standard federal limits are 80,000 pounds gross vehicle weight, 20,000 pounds on a single axle, and 34,000 pounds on a tandem axle. Federal bridge weight rules and certain exceptions can also affect how much a truck may legally carry. Limits on other roads can vary.

Rules vary by state. “Some require all commercial motor vehicles to stop, while others require only those above a certain weight to stop,” according to the Federal Highway Administration. “Ultimately, States must certify that they are enforcing their weight limits on certain highways in order not to jeopardize their receipt of Federal highway funds.”

Drivers who pull in follow signs directing them to a scale, where their trucks are weighed either while moving slowly or at a complete stop. If the weight is within the limits, they may be cleared to leave. Inspectors may still pull a truck aside for a closer look even when its weight is fine, based on screening results, visible defects, or random selection. An overweight truck may also be inspected further.

Inspectors may check a truck’s tires, brakes, lights, and cargo, along with the driver’s records. They may also review credentials and permits, such as registration and fuel-tax paperwork, along with the driver’s hours-of-service logs. “There are eight levels of inspections ranging from the Level I Inspection, which evaluates both the driver and vehicle, to inspection levels with a more specific area of focus, such as Level VI for radioactive materials and Level VIII for electronic inspections,” according to the Commercial Vehicle Safety Alliance.

Drivers of overweight trucks may receive a citation or have to move or remove some cargo before leaving. The exact consequences vary by state and violation.

More serious safety problems, like faulty brakes, can put a truck or driver out of service. A truck placed out of service can’t return to the road until the problem is fixed. Drivers placed out of service must wait until their restrictions end.

Some trucks can skip the stop altogether through electronic bypass programs. These programs use safety records and other information to determine whether a driver can continue without entering the station. Drivers still have to follow any signs or signals telling them to stop.

#7808. The Best Waterproof Gloves of 2026, Tested and Reviewed

100+ Most Unique and Practical Gifts 🎁 for Homeowners and DIYers

By Mark Wolfe, Additional research provided by Tom Scalisi

Like a rain jacket for your hands, waterproof gloves are essential gear for those working—or playing—outdoors in cold or inclement weather. For outdoor sports enthusiasts, they keep hands dry and protect against frostbite. For those who work outdoors, they are essential because they offer protection from grease, mud, and other wet messes.

We searched out a diverse collection of waterproof gloves for a wide variety of tasks in all seasons. Then we tested their ability to keep hands dry and comfortable in tough conditions. The Carhartt Waterproof Insulated Gloves earned our pick as the best waterproof gloves for men for their reliable waterproofing, comfortable insulation, and affordable price, and the MCTi Ski Gloves for Women topped our women’s picks for their watertight protection, flexible fit, and responsive touch-screen fingertips.

Bottom line: Discover the best waterproof gloves of 2026, tested for durability, comfort, and specific needs, ensuring dry and warm hands in any condition.

We initially selected the following gloves based on the quality of their construction, their durability, and the other features outlined previously. Then we tested them to discover how they held up under wet, slippery conditions. Find out how they performed in the reviews ahead.

Men looking for a long-lasting pair of gloves to keep their hands dry and warm may find what they’re looking for in Carhartt’s waterproof insulated gloves. From the shell to the liner to the palm pad, these gloves are made of 100 percent polyester. They provide a warm, durable, and waterproof barrier between the skin and the elements.

A liner made with Carhartt’s FastDry moisture-wicking technology prevents sweat from collecting inside the gloves, and a waterproof insert provides an extra layer of protection from the elements. Adjustable hook-and-loop closures and elastic cuffs keep hands snug while keeping out cold air and elements.

In our tests, these Carhartt waterproof work gloves were as comfortable as they were waterproof. They performed perfectly on all three of our waterproof tests. They stayed dry under the shower and when immersed in water while providing excellent holding ability thanks to the textured grip area. Three-dimensional construction lets the hand rest in a natural position and delivers good dexterity for gripping and holding. Although we didn’t test specifically for winter warmth, these gloves are deeply insulated for cold-weather work. However, the bulky profile takes away the ability to pick up small or thin items from a flat surface or to reach into a pants pocket.

What our tester says: “These got ‘Best Overall’ because they’re not only toasty and affordable, but they also make an excellent choice for winter chores while not looking like work gloves.”—Mark Wolfe, Product Reviews tester and writer

Get the Carhartt waterproof gloves at Amazon.

Women on the hunt for warm, waterproof gloves may want to look at MCTi’s ski gloves. They pair a polyurethane outer shell with a faux leather palm and thumb-grip area for holding ski poles or other slippery objects. On the gloves’ interior, a waterproof liner helps keep moisture from reaching the skin.

MCTi’s gloves also contain 120 grams of Thinsulate insulation that keeps hands warm in temperatures as cold as -10 degrees Fahrenheit without adding much bulk. Handy elastic wrist leashes make keeping track of the gloves easier if the wearer removes them, and sensitive touch-screen pads on three fingers allow the wearer to answer a phone or send a text without having to take off the gloves.

In our tests, these ski gloves by MCTi seemed more like general-use winter gloves. The waterproof feature is on point, with zero water intrusion during testing and a capable grip in wet conditions. Not only that, but the insulation was less puffy than some of the other gloves we tested, which improved dexterity and flexibility for gripping and handling small items. The touch-screen fingertips worked well. Moreover, they’re available in an assortment of accent colors: gray, red, white, rose, and yellow.

Get the MCTi waterproof gloves at Amazon.

Men looking for lightweight protection from the weather may want to consider Ozero’s men’s thermal gloves, which provide warmth and weather resistance without a lot of bulk. These gloves feature a water-resistant and windproof polyester construction that keeps the wearer’s hands dry and warm in inclement weather (most of the shell fabric is indeed waterproof, but the seams and touch-screen pads on two fingers are not, hence the “water-resistant” designation). This pair is a good choice for cycling, running, walking, or other outdoor pursuits.

These gloves may not be well suited to subzero temperatures, but they’re suitable for regular winter wear and have some nice features. The gloves’ thumbs and index fingers contain sensors that are touch-screen compatible, and the palms are covered in grippy silica gel pods to help users maintain a good grip on phones and other belongings. Elastic cuffs keep out the elements. These gloves fit snugly; the manufacturer suggests sizing up for a more relaxed fit.

These mid-weight lifestyle gloves are built for everyday travel and tasks in frosty weather, but not in pouring rain. Our rain simulation and immersion tests revealed numerous water entry points. Water resistance was good in our aggressive rain simulation for about a minute before leaks developed, so we believe the gloves could keep hands mostly or completely dry during an average rainstorm. They provided excellent grip for wet items. The touch-screen feature worked well, and the snug, low-profile fit allowed us to pick up a key that was lying flat on a countertop. Also note that these gloves cost less than most of the others we tested. Moreover, they are slim and flexible and easily fit into jacket pockets.

Get the Ozero waterproof gloves at Amazon or Walmart.

Leather work gloves are a necessity when working near hot surfaces and sparks in addition to protecting the hands from abrasion, cuts, and punctures. Youngstown Glove Company’s FR Waterproof Leather Utility gloves incorporate both leather and Kevlar, a synthetic fabric commonly used for protection, along with a waterproof, windproof, breathable polyurethane barrier. These gloves, which have earned American National Standards Institute (ANSI) compliance for welding, provide Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA)-approved protection for a wide range of tasks. However, they don’t provide adequate protection for electrical work.

Youngstown’s waterproof utility work gloves delivered good waterproof and wet-grip performances in our three wet tests. Although we got the leather so thoroughly wet that the gloves became heavy, the waterproof barrier prevented water intrusion to the skin. Wet grip was not a problem. We were pleasantly surprised by the dexterity that these bulky gloves provided, thanks to their three-dimensional construction and a naturally relaxed hand posture. Overall, we would not recommend these gloves for extended use in a watery environment because those conditions would cause the leather to degrade quickly. However, those who need a sturdy and comfortable insulated glove for working in the elements may want to look at these.

Get the Youngstown waterproof gloves at Amazon, JB Tools, or Youngstown Glove Company.

Carhartt’s Cold Snap insulated work gloves offer both cold-weather protection and long-lasting construction that’s tough enough for the jobsite. With warm insulation on the outer shell and a reinforced palm, these polyester gloves are reinforced with leather for extra durability. They’re waterproof and have a nose wipe on the thumb, making them a good choice for working in rough weather.

Cold Snap gloves feature some of Carhartt’s proprietary materials, including a FastDry lining for wicking moisture and Storm Defender waterproofing treatment. They have a thick cuff with an adjustable drawstring for improved weather protection. A small section of goatskin around the finger and thumb area provides added grip.

Our second pair of Carhartt waterproof work gloves performed nearly as well as the first. It provided excellent waterproof and wet-grip performance along with excellent dexterity, considering the lofty insulation. The polyester and leather exterior sheds water very well instead of becoming saturated and heavy. We liked the drawcord cuff on these gloves a little less than we liked the hook-and-loop strap closure on our “Best Overall” selection because the barrel-cord tightener is harder to manipulate with gloved hands. Nevertheless, pairing outstanding waterproofing, warmth, and comfort with a great look is the winning recipe for an all-around great pair of gloves.

Get the Carhartt Cold Snap waterproof gloves on Amazon.

No more freezing hands when you try to take a pic or return an important text. These low-profile knitted Sealskinz gloves offer triple-layer insulated waterproof, windproof protection from the elements with touch-screen-capable fingertips and outstanding range of motion. The nylon and elastane outer layer offers excellent durability with silicone-printed grips on the palm and fingers for a secure grip. A mid-layer windproof, waterproof, breathable membrane keeps the warmth in and the elements out. The lining is made of merino wool, nylon, and elastane for added warmth and breathability.

These Sealskinz gloves offered a lot of things we really liked but a few things we didn’t. We appreciated that they were truly 100 percent waterproof, both in our simulated rain test and when immersed in water. They also offer outstanding wet-grip capability, with touch-perfect touch-screen functionality. The low-profile design, moderate amount of insulation, and superior wet performance are perfect for getting outside on those miserable raw days when it’s 30 degrees Fahrenheit with freezing rain. But we didn’t love the semi-absorbent exterior because it holds on to more than its share of water, even though the water never reached our hands. It makes these otherwise excellent gloves feel heavy and a little bit squelchy. However, these may be the best gloves when wet weather threatens.

Get the Sealskinz waterproof gloves at Amazon or Sealskinz.

Hestra’s Army Leather Heli Ski 3-Finger Gloves are designed for men and women who spend their time atop some of the coldest mountains. These three-finger gloves are constructed from Hestra’s windproof, breathable, and water-resistant Triton fabric, with goat leather on the palms and fingers for improved grip in cold and slippery conditions.

The insides of these Hestra gloves are made of a very thin polyester fiber with efficient insulating properties, which makes them warm without being overly bulky. The oversize cuffs feature a drawstring closure to keep out snow and moisture, and leashes ensure the gloves won’t get lost. These Army Leather Heli gloves are available in three colors.

These gloves looked great and performed better than expected in our tests, but they were not totally waterproof. We anticipated soaking-wet hands because of the leather and “water- resistant” fabric. In our tests, the leather eventually became wet, and some moisture from outside did seep inside. They offered an OK but not great grip when wet. The best advantages of these gloves are the finger configuration, which offers better warmth than a conventional glove and better articulation than a mitten. That said, we did not test for performance in cold weather. On the downside, the leather must be regularly oiled (a tube is included), and they take a long time to dry once wet.

Get the Hestra Heli waterproof gloves at Amazon, REI, or Backcountry.com.

Built in the style of traditional cuff-length work gloves, Hestra Job Titan Flex Gloves bring the outstanding comfort and durability of goatskin leather with waterproof neoprene cuffs and Hestra Flex fabric. The stress points on the palm and fingers are reinforced with double-layered leather, while the index fingers and thumbs feature touch-screen pads for convenience. These three-season work gloves are lined with moisture-wicking fleece for added warmth and comfort in cold, wet weather.

In our tests, these gloves provided good waterproof protection and excellent wet-gripping ability. They resisted water penetration for over a minute before moisture found its entry point at the edges of the touch-screen pad on the index finger. The touch-screen pad functioned well, and the glove offered good dexterity and comfort overall, but the sizing runs a bit small. The moderate price point and durable construction make them ideal spring, fall, or mild winter weather general-use work gloves.

Get the Hestra Titan waterproof gloves at Amazon.

We selected and tested a diverse assortment of waterproof gloves designed for a variety of uses in different seasons. For all of them, our key testing consideration was whether the gloves were truly waterproof. To find out, we used three testing methods and allowed the gloves to thoroughly dry between tests. All comments about sizing are subjective, based on sizing guides provided by the manufacturers and perceived comfort by the tester. On those gloves not listed as unisex, women tested women’s gloves, and men tested men’s gloves.

First, we simulated storm conditions with a rain-wand attachment on a garden hose. The testers wore each pair of gloves beneath a steady 2-minute shower, flexing their hands and turning them over to expose all parts of the gloves to the stream. In the second test, we immersed our gloved hands into a bucket of water, again flexing and rotating to ensure that they were completely wet. Finally, we tested them for wet-gripping ability while handling smooth wet stones. To merit inclusion in this guide, each pair of gloves passed all three tests with minimal water intrusion to the inside of the glove.

Before shopping for the best waterproof gloves, consider the type of work planned for the gloves as well as the kind of materials and construction desired. In this section, we review some key considerations to keep in mind while shopping for the best waterproof gloves, including materials, use, fit, and more.

Choosing the best waterproof gloves depends on how they’ll be used. Work gloves are completely different from those intended for outdoor sports or casual wear.

On garments labeled “waterproof,” the outer shell is usually where the magic happens. Materials like tightly woven nylon, polyester, softshell technical materials, treated leather, and others work well to shed water before it can seep through to the lining. Keep in mind that it’s very rare for leather gloves to actually be waterproof; more likely, they are simply water-resistant.

Aside from shell material, other elements in waterproof gloves’ exteriors make them useful in wet or messy situations. Some of the best waterproof gloves, for example, have textured grips that make it easier for the wearer to grab on to wet, slippery surfaces, making them ideal for skiing, cycling, and other active pursuits. Those looking for waterproof gloves for work may want to invest in gloves with reinforced palms and thumbs, which should last longer and stand up to more wear.

The best waterproof gloves contain an optional outer shell with conductors that transfer the electrical charge from a finger to a touch screen, allowing users to manipulate their phones without removing their gloves.

Some of the best waterproof gloves contain insulation that captures body heat, which forms air pockets that warm with the heat from the hand. Most insulation is a man-made poly-fill material such as Thinsulate or 3M.

To ensure gloves keep warm air inside and cold air from seeping in, some waterproof gloves have long elastic cuffs that hug tight to the wrist and arm, closing off any pathway for air to enter. For even warmer gloves, look for removable liners that can slip inside a waterproof glove to add another layer of insulation.

When selecting the best waterproof gloves, fit and comfort are essential. However, a “good fit” is relative to the activity. A pair of running gloves fits quite differently than a pair of winter work gloves or ski gloves.

Waterproof running or hiking gloves often feel like a stretchy, flexible second skin. Because they’re lightweight and wick away moisture, users sometimes forget they’re even wearing them.

Waterproof work gloves are bulkier and a bit stiff because they’re generally made from thick nylon or leather that resists ripping, tearing, and friction. Moreover, extra padding or reinforcement on the thumbs or palms can add to their bulk. Though work gloves fit loosely, they shouldn’t be so loose that it’s difficult to pick up small items while wearing them.

Ski gloves are flexible but don’t wear particularly well because they’re typically made from materials like nylon. Properly fitting ski gloves fit snugly around the wrist but are roomy enough to allow the skier to manipulate straps on ski poles and boot bindings.

Also consider breathability. If hands sweat and moisture collects inside the glove, it won’t matter that the shell is waterproof because hands will still get wet. Breathable gloves help some of the heat and moisture escape without letting in cold outer air and moisture.

Now that you know a bit more about the factors to consider when choosing the best waterproof gloves for your needs, some questions may remain. The following are some of the most frequently asked questions about the best waterproof gloves, so check for an answer to your question below.

Waterproof means that absolutely no water makes its way into the glove. Water-resistant means that the gloves shed water to a degree before water comes in.

As one of the best options for the warmest waterproof gloves, the Carhartt Cold Snap waterproof gloves are warm enough to protect your hands in very cold temperatures.

You can wash some waterproof gloves, but it’s best to spot clean them and use a boot dryer with a glove attachment if they become soiled.

The best way to dry the inside of waterproof gloves is to put them on a boot dryer with a glove attachment.

#7807. If You See a Taco Bell With THIS On It, Here’s What It Means

A strange metal frame on some new Taco Bell restaurants has people wondering if construction crews forgot something. Here's what it's for.

There are certain restaurant chain designs everyone has come to recognize. McDonald’s golden arches. Pizza Hut’s red roof. But what about the open framing on the side of new Taco Bell buildings?

If you haven’t seen the new Taco Bell design, it includes open framing on the second floor on one side. But why? A recent Reddit post sparked plenty of guesses about what the framing was for.

New Taco Bell Building – What’s the Open Framing? by u/Kindly_Blueberry2814 in whatisit

The design seems to be more aesthetic than functional and is part of Taco Bell’s newer restaurant design, known as Kitchen X. It is part of the company’s move away from its older Spanish-style buildings, which featured arches and stucco exteriors.

“That open metal cage on the left is just decorative framing to make the building look sleek and balanced,” one Reddit user commented. “The left side of the restaurant has lower ceilings for storage, coolers, and the drive-thru lane, so they added that hollow steel frame on top to match the height of the main dining room on the right. There are no stairs or deck up there, just standard roof stuff and AC units hidden behind the wall.”

Another commenter agreed, saying, “It’s just an architectural design feature to give visual balance.”

Taco Bell has introduced Kitchen X at select locations across the United States, including new restaurants in Carver and Rochester, Minnesota. However, the exterior can vary between locations, so not every restaurant has the same framing.

Before Reddit users settled on the decorative explanation, they had plenty of other guesses.

“It’s to land the tacocopter,” one Reddit user joked.

“Future terrace dining,” another Reddit user speculated.

The discussion also turned into a debate about Taco Bell’s changing appearance. Some users said they missed the chain’s older buildings with more character, while others shared photos of former locations with more traditional designs.

Whether you love or hate the look, there’s no denying that it’s eye-popping and hard to miss. Which is probably what the company was hoping for when coming up with the new look.

#7806. Crucial Snow Blower Maintenance Tasks to Complete Before the First Snow

100+ Most Unique and Practical Gifts 🎁 for Homeowners and DIYers

Published Nov 21, 2026 10:00 AM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Tips, tricks & ideas for a better home and yard, delivered to your inbox daily.

Imagine your frustration when your driveway is covered in snow after the first winter storm, but your snow blower won’t start. As winter approaches, it’s time to make sure your snow blower is ready to tackle that first snowfall. You’ll want to take a few steps to check that it’s tuned up and ready to go without a hitch. We spoke to Sean Dwyer, senior product manager for commercial and residential wheeled products at Husqvarna Group North America to identify the top snow blower maintenance tasks to prioritize so you are prepared when the first snowflake falls.

By far the most important step is to make sure you have a fresh supply of fuel, says Dwyer. “If you have regular pump fuel, it should be less than 30 days old, and ideally premium grade that’s a non-ethanol blend,” he explains. Fuel can go stale over time and gum up the snow blower’s carburetor. Dwyer recommends running the unit out of gas before storing it. “Otherwise, at a minimum, purchase stabilized canned fuel or add a fuel stabilizer.” Gasoline with a stabilizer typically lasts for about 4 to 6 months.

Spend some time reviewing the key components of the unit. “This means checking engine oil and tire pressures, and also starting the unit to ensure proper wheel drive and auger operation,” notes Dwyer. “This is also a good time to shut the fuel off and run the carburetor dry to give your snow blower the best chance of a successful operation when you need it.”

In addition, pay attention to these additional parts of the snow blower:

Featuring an easy-to-pour package and effective formula, this motor oil washes dirt and deposits out of the engine as it passes through.

Battery-powered snow blowers are convenient, but it’s important to recognize that cold weather and batteries don’t typically work well together, warns Dwyer. Checking battery health is part of regular snow blower maintenance. Rechargeable batteries can degrade over time, and won’t be able to hold as much charge as they age as they do when new. He recommends keeping fully charged batteries in the house or a location where they will remain above freezing temperatures. “If everything is in the cold garage, there is a good chance they won’t work when you need them to,” he explains. “Also, remember that when you are done, bring the batteries back to a warm place so they are ready to go next time.”

Snow blowers typically contain shear bolts (also called pins) as a safety feature. The shear bolts are designed to break to protect the auger gears from damage if the unit runs into hard objects like ice from a blizzard. There is typically one pin on each auger and one or two on the impeller.

To change these components, wear protective gloves. “With the engine shut off, try to rotate each individual auger by hand,” says Dwyer. “You should not be able to rotate the augers, and the shear bolts will be visually present.” To check the impeller, look for the shear bolts, or hold one of the augers firmly, and slowly try to turn the impeller. “Be careful when checking the impeller, as it is tied to the shaft that will drive the augers.”

If these items spin freely, the shear bolt is likely damaged or missing, says Dwyer. Replace any missing or broken bolts to protect your snow blower. It’s a good idea to always keep a stash of shear bolts on hand.

Designed to wear down with use, skid shoes help keep a snow blower’s housing at the correct height and also protect your pavement. They are located on the lower sides of the auger housing and are designed to hold the scraper, located at the bottom of the auger housing, just above the ground, says Dwyer. “As these shoes wear, the scraper will contact the ground and wear will increase,” he explains.

“A simple way to adjust the shoes is to sit the snow blower scraper on something around ¼ inch thick, like a paint stir stick, and then loosen the bolts holding the shoes to adjust them down to contact the ground and retighten,” suggests Dwyer.

After months of scouring the market and putting products through their paces, we’ve named the best of the best in new tools. There’s something for everyone, from veteran pros to average Joes.

#7805. LeBron James sues sports betting startup over unauthorized use of ‘Bron’ nickname

NBA superstar LeBron James is suing the makers of sports betting app Bron, claiming that it is intentionally ripping off his nickname. (Photo from Shutterstock)

NBA superstar LeBron James is suing the makers of sports betting app Bron, claiming that it is intentionally ripping off his nickname.

In a federal complaint filed Tuesday in the Southern District of New York, James said he has been known as “Bron” since he was a young basketball standout in Ohio. He alleges that PlayVision and its co-founders, Anish Gupta and Marc Zoghby, seek “to trade on” his “valuable name and reputation” by naming their app Bron.

There is no other connection between the word and the defendants or any other feature of their app, James alleges. He also argues in the complaint that when the defendants launched a marketing campaign for the Bron app earlier this month, they used a video advertisement that incorporated an artificial intelligence-generated version of him.

“The AI-generated version of Mr. James sits in an NBA-style locker room wearing a basketball jersey bearing Mr. James’s nickname, ‘Bron,’ above the number ‘23’—a number associated with Mr. James and the one he currently wears on the Philadelphia 76ers—with physical traits that mimic Mr. James, down to his identifiable tattoos,” according to the complaint.

“Speaking in Mr. James’s voice, the AI-generated Mr. James scrolls through wagers on other NBA players in defendants’ Bron app,” the complaint continues. “The ad then urges viewers to ‘scroll to bet.’”

The lawsuit seeks damages and an injunction preventing the defendants from using the “Bron” name; James’ name, image and likeness; and voice.

Courthouse News Service has additional reporting.

A representative for Bron did not respond to the publication’s request for comment.

#7803. Gun Rights and Guilt by Association

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

Some excerpts from the longish opinion today in Shilling v. County of San Diego, decided today by Ninth Circuit Judge Patrick Bumatay, joined by Judges Kenneth Lee and Jennifer Sung:

The San Diego County Sheriff revoked Kenneth Shilling's concealed-carry weapon ("CCW") license over his affiliation with the Boozefighters Motorcycle Club…. [We conclude, among other things, that] the district court improperly dismissed his First Amendment [freedom of association] claim….

Kenneth Charles Shilling resides in San Diego, California. He's a member of the Boozefighters Motorcycle Club, which, according to Shilling, was founded in 1946 by World War II veterans. In his view, it's not like some other motorcycle clubs, which are known for criminal and gang activity. Instead, the Boozefighters focus on charitable work and the "core values of family, work, and community." Shilling's record is clean; he has no criminal history.

In June 2022, when the "good moral character" requirement [for getting a concealed carry license] still existed [under California law], Shilling applied for and received a CCW license from then-San Diego County Sheriff Anthony Ray. This was short lived. Less than a year and a half later, in December 2023, a different San Diego County Sheriff, Kelly Martinez, used the "good moral character" requirement to revoke Shilling's CCW license. In a letter notifying Shilling of the revocation, Sheriff Martinez explained that the "San Diego Sheriff's Department['s] good moral character definition" excludes a person who:

Has a pattern of or propensity for criminal conduct, as demonstrated by anything in the application or investigation for a license. This includes, but is not limited to, evidence of criminal behavior or a close nexus to a criminal gang. In making this determination, the Sheriff's Department shall use an objective inquiry, considering the facts and circumstances known at the time of the application or through the investigation.

The letter said that Shilling's license was revoked due to his association with the Boozefighters Motorcycle Club, which the Sheriff described as a "criminal street gang." Shilling was not given the opportunity to contest the allegations before his license was revoked, but he could request reconsideration of the decision. The new CCW regime with the "dangerousness" requirement took effect on January 1, 2024, shortly after Shilling's license was revoked….

Here's the court's analysis allowing Shilling's First Amendment freedom of association claim to go forward:

The First Amendment guarantees all Americans the "right to associate with others." … [T]he right protects groups of individuals "in pursuit of a wide variety of political, social, economic, educational, religious and cultural ends." …

The government may infringe the freedom of association in "varied ways," including by "punish[ing] individuals for their affiliations." The government cannot impose "criminal sanctions or deny[ ] rights and privileges solely because of a citizen's association with an unpopular organization." For example, a group of students could not be denied the "benefits" of official campus recognition at a state college merely because of its affiliation with a national organization associated with disruptive and violent campus activity…. [Likewise,] "Civil liability may not be imposed merely because an individual belonged to a group, some members of which committed acts of violence." … If the government seeks to deprive an individual of a benefit, privilege, or right based on association with an alleged criminal organization, "it is necessary to establish that the group itself possessed unlawful goals and that the individual held a specific intent to further those illegal aims." …

Given this understanding of the First Amendment, Shilling easily pleaded a violation of his freedom of association…. [His] allegations sufficiently raise an infringement of Shilling's free-association right because the Sheriff deprived him of a benefit, privilege, or right—the ability to carry a concealed weapon in public—"solely because of [his] association with an unpopular organization." Unless the Sheriff adequately meets her burden of showing the Boozefighters "possessed unlawful goals" and Shilling's "specific intent to further those illegal aims," she cannot "punish [Shilling] for [his] affiliations." This kind of "guilt by association alone, without establishing that an individual's association poses the threat feared by the Government, is an impermissible basis upon which to deny First Amendment rights."

In dismissing this claim, the district court misunderstood the nature of the free-association right. It asserted that Shilling had to show the revocation of his CCW license somehow prevented him from associating with the Boozefighters Motorcycle Club or participating in the Club's activities. While preventing an individual from participating in a group's lawful activities may be one way to violate the First Amendment right, it's infringed in "varied ways." And "denying" an individual benefits, rights, or privileges "solely because of [his] association"—as Shilling alleges—is certainly another way….

For the court's analysis of sovereign immunity and of whether Schilling's Second Amendment claim was moot, see the full opinion.

Gary W. Gorski (Veterans Law Center) represents plaintiff.

#7802. You Can Actually Repair a House in GTA6—But How Realistic Is It?

GTA6 let's you take a break from a life of crime to make some much-needed home repairs on Jason and Lucia's house.

Just in case your algorithm is different from mine, here’s some news: Grand Theft Auto 6 officially released today. After 13 years of waiting, fans of the open-world action-adventure video game series can finally dive into a new, richly detailed and fully realized virtual world. Boot up the game, and you’ll find yourself faced with surprising realism, a world of crime, and the ability to do just about whatever you want. That’s right, even… DIY home improvement jobs?

Yep, you’re reading that right. As part of its commitment to realism, GTA developer Rockstar Games has given players the ability to do some honest-to-goodness, roll-up-your-sleeves-and-get-to-work home improvement virtually.

And it’s not just a short cutscene where you see the house magically go from disrepair to fully fixed up. You, as the player, have to actually do the work, whether you’re drywalling, painting, or roofing. Luckily, it’s just a video game because the game is also set in a fictional version of Florida in the summer, which is probably one of the last places on earth you’d want to be stuck doing any sort of construction work.

Let’s take a look at a few of the home improvement jobs done by GTA6‘s Jason Duval and see if his work meets Family Handyman’s standards.

With his lady friend Lucia on the way back from prison, Jason decides to fix up the place… including the unfinished framing in the center of his living room. Luckily, Jason knows how to hang drywall. The gameplay represents the job pretty accurately— Jason holds the drywall in place and screws it into the studs with an impact driver. We don’t get to see any taping or mudding, though. 7/10

Next, we’ll inspect whether Jason should perhaps prioritize a career as a painter over his life of crime. The painting section is also pretty accurate to the average DIY painting experience. Jason has to choose between three different color options before pouring the paint into a tray and using a roller to paint the wall. It’s pretty boring, which is honestly just like painting in real life — so bonus points for immersive realism. 8/10

One of the first things Jason knows he has to fix before Lucia arrives is the massive hole in his roof that’s letting in a near-constant drip of rain. Luckily, like a lot of DIYers, he has some roofing experience, a cordless nail gun and a stack of shingles just lying around for some reason. Again, this section is pretty realistic. If gamers want the full Florida roofing experience, though, they’ll have to crank their heaters to maximum or perhaps play the game in a sauna. 6/10

Look, I get it. The Grand Theft Auto series is about living out fantasies, providing gamers a sandbox where they can virtually experience the impossible.

But still… “House repairs complete” is a bridge too far. Ask any DIYer, and they will tell you no house is ever fully repaired. Pretending home improvement work could ever be finished is just not realistic and really took me out of the experience. 3/10.

Overall, the game is cool. But to be honest, I’m not sure what the point is now that the house repairs are complete.

Thankfully, experts in the home decor space are sharing their seasonal tips to help you get ready.

HGTV’s Jonathan Scott shared a video with a few Christmas decorating hacks he and his partner, Zooey Deschanel, use in their home.

“I like it to be a little bit nostalgic, a little bit fun, and a whole lot of holiday spirit,” Scott says.

There’s no one right way to decorate for Christmas, and even if so that doesn’t mean you should stick to the conventional script, according to Scott. “There are lots of different rules when decorating for the holidays, but of course, as we know, rules are meant to be broken,” Scott says. “So it really depends on your comfort level.”

Even the nicest artificial trees can look a little too perfect. Scott’s trick is to stuff a few extra branches into the tree, leaving some sticking out at random. He also adds more lights, including larger bulbs, even though his tree is already pre-lit.

Scott has been collecting nutcrackers for years, and yes, he even names them. Rather than display them the same way every Christmas, he changes things up with different garlands, beads, and branches. It’s a way to get a new look out of decorations he already owns.

Those giant stacked presents in Scott’s house look like they’d be a pain to store, but they’re not. Each box fits inside the next, so the whole display takes up a fraction of the space once Christmas is over.

You can watch the full video and get more tips here:

At the top of everyone’s mind around the holidays should be safety.

Scott recommends being mindful of fragile decorations, especially if you have young children or large pets. Glass ornaments and other breakable decorations can easily get knocked over, so consider using sturdier pieces in areas where kids and pets spend a lot of time.

The U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission (CPSC) also recommends looking for a “fire resistant” label when purchasing an artificial Christmas tree and regularly watering live trees to reduce fire risks.

Whether you’re adding a few new touches to your favorite decorations or going all out with a Christmas tree in every room, the most important thing is creating a space that feels festive to you.

#7798. Second Amendment as a Right to Sell Guns as Well as to Have and Buy Them?

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

From Fifth Circuit Judges James Ho and Andrew Oldham in an unsigned opinion filed yesterday in U.S. v. Deare:

Jeremiah Deare was indicted for conspiracy to engage in the business of dealing firearms without a federal firearms license in violation of 18 U.S.C. § 922(a)(1) and for making false statements with respect to records of licensed firearms dealers. Deare then filed a motion to dismiss the indictment, broadly challenging the constitutionality of § 922(a)(1)'s licensure requirement and related record-keeping requirements.

The district court denied his motion to dismiss, holding that federal licensing and record-keeping requirements are not implicated by the Second Amendment because such requirements do not affect an individual's right to keep or bear arms. The court further held that, even if federal licensing requirements are implicated by the Second Amendment, such requirements are consistent with our Nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation….

Deare primarily challenges the district court's denial of his motion to dismiss the indictment. Specifically, he argues that the Second Amendment's plain text covers firearm sales, and that § 922(a)(1)'s licensure requirement and related record-keeping requirements are inconsistent with our Nation's history of firearm regulation.

The plain text of the Second Amendment covers the sale of firearms. As we noted in Reese v. BATFE (5th Cir. 2025), "the right to 'keep and bear arms' surely implies the right to purchase them." During oral argument, the government conceded that the Second Amendment applies to the commercial sale of firearms.

Accordingly, we vacate the district court's order denying Deare's motion to dismiss the indictment and remand to the district court for further proceedings.

(As I read the opinion, it doesn't affect the false statements charge.)

It's gratifying that our court today reaffirms what we should have long understood—that the Second Amendment right to "keep and bear Arms" plainly encompasses the sale of arms as well. It seems obvious that constitutional rights are meaningless if the Government can simply prohibit the means by which citizens are able to exercise those rights.

Our dissenting colleague theorizes that 18 U.S.C. § 922(a) is not about constitutional rights, but about commercial regulation. It's the same view expressed by the district court below: "§ 922(a)(1) is a modest regulation of the commercial activity of selling/transferring firearms to others…. [F]ederal licensure and record keeping requirements do not affect an individual's rights to possess firearms…. [T]hese requirements affect only the seller. As such, Defendants have failed to persuade this Court that these commercial licensure and recordkeeping requirements implicate the Second Amendment."

Or as the dissent puts it simply, "the Second Amendment … doesn't mention sellers," so "I do not think that the sellers of guns are covered."

By that logic, the First Amendment doesn't mention sellers, so presumably booksellers aren't covered by the First Amendment, either. But that can't be right.

Constitutional rights are constitutional rights, regardless of whether they're compensated—as I've noted on a number of occasions. And if that's true under the First Amendment, then it should be equally true in Second Amendment challenges to § 922(a) as well….

Our dissenting colleague responds by offering a textual distinction between the First and Second Amendments. At bottom, the dissent theorizes that the "freedom of speech" contemplates sales, whereas "the right of the people to keep and bear Arms" does not. But with respect, I don't see the textual distinction that she sees. The theory is also hard to square with what we saw in Villarreal.…

Judge Oldham, joined by Judge Ho, concurred in the judgment (though presumably they also joined their own unsigned opinion):

The first question presented is whether restrictions on the sale of firearms burden the Second Amendment rights of American citizens. They do—in at least two ways. First, such restrictions directly burden the seller's right to keep and bear arms. And second, they burden the prospective buyer's right to keep and bear arms, because the right to keep an item always includes the right to acquire it.

Start with the constitutional text. The Second Amendment does not just prohibit the government from denying the right to keep and bear arms. Instead, it says that the right cannot be "infringed." And at the Founding, "infringe" meant "violate," "destroy," or "hinder." Thus, the government cannot hinder the people's rights to keep and bear arms.

Restrictions on sale hinder both the seller's and buyer's right to keep and bear arms. Start with the seller's right to possess firearms. The Second Amendment guarantees the right to keep guns for personal use, and the seller is an individual who can lawfully possess guns. And it's hornbook property law that the right to possess an article "includes the right to acquire, use, and dispose of it." So the right to keep a gun must include the right to dispose of that gun as the owner sees fit. This is not an independent "right to sell." Rather, my point is that governmental interference with the right to sell a firearm is itself a burden on the seller's existing property right in that firearm. It hinders and hence infringes the seller's rights.

The same logic applies to the buyer. The buyer's ability to keep and bear arms is certainly "infringed" by regulations that hinder the purchase of arms. After all, the Supreme Court has explained that inherent in "property" is the "right to acquire, use, and dispose of it." In other words, a restriction on the sale of weapons obviously impacts the buyer's constitutional rights to acquire weapons. As one scholar has explained it:

Because one cannot 'keep' or 'bear' something without acquiring it, the act of acquiring arms must be included in the Second Amendment's 'right to keep and bear arms.' This is true for the same reason that the right to speak would be largely ineffective if it did not include the right to engage in financial transactions that are the incidents of its exercise. For there comes a point at which the regulation of action intimately and unavoidably connected with a right is a regulation of the right itself.

Joseph G.S. Greenlee, The American Tradition of Self-Made Arms, 54 St. Mary's L.J. 35 (2023).

This principle is not limited to the Second Amendment context. For example, consider the neighboring First Amendment. The Free Speech Clause "afford[s] the public access to discussion, debate, and the dissemination of information and ideas"—and thus clearly protects the right to sell and distribute speech, including speech written or produced by others. And it protects the recipient's right to receive information and ideas. Willis v. Town of Marshall (9th Cir. 2002) (Kozinski, J., concurring) ("[T]he right to hear and the right to speak are flip sides of the same coin."). Without a right to provide speech, there is no right to receive information and ideas.

Likewise, consider the Free Exercise Clause. "[T]he text of the Free Exercise Clause gives a specific group of people (those who wish to engage in the 'exercise of religion') the right to do so without hindrance." It is axiomatic that the right to free exercise of religion includes the right to practice it with others in, for example, houses of worship. Shutting down houses of worship is an obvious First Amendment violation for many reasons—not the least of which is that it prevents the faithful from communing with each other and with church leaders who provide teaching, holy sacraments, and other sacred traditions. Thus, the right to exercise religion includes a First Amendment freedom to participate in religious services with—and provide religious services to—others.

These examples demonstrate clear principles. A right to property, free speech, corporate worship, and firearms includes the right to provide these things. And to acquire them….

Judge Oldham also discussed the proper scope of a Fifth Circuit decision, U.S. v. Peterson (5th Cir. 2025) and concludes that it (1) "was wrong and should be overturned" and in any event (2) doesn't apply here; for more on that, read the full opinion.

I do not think that the sellers of guns are covered by the Second Amendment (which doesn't mention sellers) …. {Second Amendment is quite different from the First Amendment mentioned in the concurrence. The First Amendment states "freedom of speech" and lists people in general which is quite large whereas the Second Amendment says "the right of people to keep and bear Arms" not mentioning selling Arms or all situations.}

[But] I am respectful of the majority opinion on that given our prior cases and what the government said. So, even assuming arguendo the sellers are covered, I see nothing in this case that shows that the rules for the sellers in this context are inappropriate and, therefore, unconstitutional. Also, to me, since Deare did not properly challenge the relevant rules to show that they are abusive, I do not see a need to remand on that. To me, the relevant rules as to him are sufficient and proper, so I would simply affirm.

I appreciate Judge Ho's and Judge Oldham's arguments that the right to keep and bear arms must include the right to acquire them, which in turn means that restrictions on sales must be evaluated to make sure they don't improperly burden the rights of would-be buyers. By way of analogy, the Court continues to recognize a right to use contraceptives (see Griswold v. Connecticut). Surely that must mean that a ban on selling contraceptives would unconstitutionally burden the would-be buyers' rights, and even less comprehensive restrictions on selling them might likewise be seen as too burdensome.

But I'm skeptical of the argument that the Second Amendment secures a right of sellers independent of the right of buyers. A bookseller may be said to be engaged in "speech" in the sense that conveying ideas to readers is a form of speech (including when one conveys them in exchange for money). A gun seller, on the other hand, isn't actually "keeping" a gun or "bearing" it. And though property rights do generally include the right to convey, including by sale, I don't think the Second Amendment should be seen as constitutionalizing that

By way of analogy, the law bans transferring guns to felons. That, the Court has said, is presumptively constitutional, because felons don't have the right to possess guns (focusing on the rights of the would-be gun possessor). But I don't think it follows that the law even implicates the right of gun sellers. When the law bans me from selling a gun to a felon, it isn't affecting my own ability to keep or bear the gun at all.

And this distinction between (1) the Second Amendment protecting gun sales as facilitative of the buyer's ability to have a gun, and (2) the Second Amendment gun sales as protecting the seller's own Second Amendment rights, may be practically significant. Under theory 1, there would likely be more room for regulation of sellers, since restrictions that only very modestly affect the buyer's ability to buy guns might then be viewed as presumptively constitutional. (That's consistent with D.C. v. Heller's statement that "nothing in our opinion should be taken to cast doubt on … laws imposing conditions and qualifications on the commercial sale of arms"). Under theory 2, there would be less room for regulation of sellers, since the sellers' own rights would be at stake as well.

Again, that's also how the distinction might play out as to the right to use contraceptives, and how it played out as to abortion in the pre-Dobbs Roe/Casey era. For instance, the right to abortion was consistent with licensure requirements for people or organizations that perform abortions, so long as this didn't unduly interfere with women's ability to get abortions. Likewise, it seems to me, the Second Amendment right to keep and bear arms is consistent with licensure requirements for gun sellers, so long as it doesn't unduly interfere with people's ability to get guns that they can then keep and bear.

#7796. En Banc Fifth Circuit Declares House COVID Proxy Voting Rule Unconstitutional

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

While purporting to offer narrow relief confined to a limited portion of the bill in Texas, the court places a bullseye on broad legislation.

Today, in Texas v. Blanche, the en banc U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit concluded that the proxy voting rule adopted by the House of Representatives during the COVID-19 pandemic violated the Quorum Clause.

The opinion, by Judge Wilson, joined by Chief Judge Elrod and Judges Jones, Smith, Willett, Ho, Duncan, Engelhardt, and Oldham begins:

During the COVID-19 pandemic, the House of Representatives adopted a rule allowing Members to record their presence by proxy for purposes of establishing a quorum. The House used this rule when passing the Consolidated Appropriations Act of 2023 (the Act), having mustered a quorum by counting hundreds of otherwise absent Members as present by proxy. The Senate then passed the bill, and the President signed it into law.

The State of Texas argues that the House's proxy-presence rule is inconsistent with the Constitution's Quorum Clause, which would mean that the House did not validly pass the Act. See U.S. Const. art. I, § 5, cl. 1. Based on that proposition, Texas seeks injunctive relief against just one portion of the Act: The Pregnant Workers Fairness Act (PWFA). The federal Government responds that the enrolled-bill rule, which instructs that a bill's passage through the legislature is conclusive proof of its authenticity, precludes judicial review of whether the Act's passage complied with the Quorum Clause. Alternatively, the Government argues that the Quorum Clause permits proxy presence.

The district court held that the enrolled-bill rule did not apply and that the House's passage of the Act—through use of the proxy-presence rule —violated the Quorum Clause. Accordingly, the district court enjoined the Government from enforcing the PWFA against Texas.

We conclude that the enrolled-bill rule does not bar our review because Texas's constitutional challenge does not implicate a dispute of fact regarding the Act's passage. We further conclude that the Act's passage was unconstitutional because the Quorum Clause does not allow proxies to be included when establishing a quorum. The Clause's text, context, original understanding, and unbroken historical application all indicate that Members of Congress must be present for quorum purposes—as the Supreme Court expressly held over 125 years ago, and as Congress has done ever since the Founding. "Proxy presence" does not count. While the chambers of the legislature have much discretion regarding their rules of procedure, the Quorum Clause's constraints on congressional power cannot be circumvented by congressional fiat. We therefore affirm the judgment of the district court.

The enrolled-bill doctrine articulated in Marshall Field does not preclude judicial review of Texas's Quorum Clause challenge. There are no disputed facts regarding the House's passage of the Act such that we would need to sift any extrinsic evidence. On the contrary, the parties agree that the House purportedly established a quorum only because it counted hundreds of proxies as "present." Texas's challenge therefore depends solely on the Quorum Clause's proper meaning.

Through that lens, the House's passage of the Consolidated Appropriations Act of 2023 contravened the Quorum Clause. The Clause's text, context, original understanding, and historical application all indicate that proxies may not be counted to establish a quorum. As the Supreme Court has held, and as Congress had previously done for over 230 years, Members must be present to satisfy the Quorum Clause. Presence-by-proxy does not suffice. An absent Member's assignment of his or her proxy cannot render that Member present for purposes of the Quorum Clause. Texas has carried its burden to show that it is entitled to a permanent injunction against the PWFA.

Judge Graves wrote the dissent, joined by Judges Stewart, Richman, Southwick, Higginson, Douglas, and Ramirez. It begins:

In this suit, the State of Texas sought a preliminary injunction preventing enforcement of one portion of the Consolidated Appropriations Act of 2023, the Pregnant Workers Fairness Act (PWFA), attempting to veto Congress's protections for pregnant workers and new parents while retaining millions in federal funding.

On May 15, 2020, in response to the COVID-19 pandemic, the House of Representatives adopted House Resolution 965, which authorized remote committee proceedings and remote voting in the House. Resolution 965 provides that:

1. [A]t any time after the Speaker . . . is notified . . . that a public health emergency due to a novel coronavirus is in effect, the Speaker . . . may designate a period . . . during which a Member who is designated by another Member as proxy in accordance with section 2 may cast the vote of such other Member or record the presence of such other Member in the House.

H.R. Res. 965 § 1(a), 116th Cong. (2020).

Section 2 described the process for remote participation through designating proxies: the designating Member had to submit a signed letter to the Clerk that specified the designated Member. Id. § 2. Section 3 outlined the process for voting during covered periods, which, absent an extension, ran for forty-five days after the Speaker, or their designee, designated such a period. Id. §§ 1(b), 3. Section 4 authorized remote Committee proceedings. Id. § 4. Section 5 mandated that the chair of the Committee on House Administration certify that it would be feasible to use technology to conduct remote voting in the House, required that the chair of the Committee on Rules submit regulations providing for the implementation of remote voting, and provided for remote voting once those regulations were in place. Id. § 5. Section 6 required that Sections 1, 2, and 3 be carried out in accordance with existing House rules to the extent practicable. Id. § 6. During the 117th Congress, the House reaffirmed this practice in House Resolution 8 and continued to apply it. H.R. Res. 8 § 3(s), 117th Cong. (2021).

At issue here: the House used these procedures as it voted on and passed the Consolidated Appropriations Act of 2023. See 168 Cong. Rec. H10,529 (daily ed. Dec. 23, 2022). Under House rules, a quorum of the 435-Member House is a simple majority: 218. See, e.g., Rules of the House of Representatives, R. XX, cl. 6(b), H.R. Doc. No. 116-177, at 873–74 (2021). The vote on the final passage of the Act was 225 yeas, 201 nays, 1 "present," and 4 non-votes. 168 Cong. Rec. H10,528 (daily ed. Dec. 23, 2022). Out of the 431 votes, 205 votes were cast by Members in person and 226 were cast remotely by proxy. See id. at H10,529.

Even though less than a majority was physically present at the time of the vote, no Member objected that a quorum was lacking. Id. Representative Chip Roy of Texas, however, noted that a physical quorum was not present and reserved the right to object. Id. In response to a series of parliamentary inquiries from Representative Roy as to how a quorum was present, the Speaker Pro Tempore, Representative G.K. Butterfield, responded that a quorum was present because "Members casting their vote or recording their presence by proxy [we]re counted for the purpose of establishing a quorum" pursuant to House Resolution 8. Id.

After the Act passed the House, presiding officers of both chambers of Congress printed and signed the bill. See 1 U.S.C. § 106. At that point, it was an "enrolled bill." Id. The enrolled bill was then sent to the President, who signed the Consolidated Appropriations Act of 2023 into law. See Pub. L. No. 117-328, 136 Stat. 4459 (2022).

The $1.7 trillion-dollar government funding bill was passed in accordance with House Rules, including House Resolution 8, which allowed members to record their presence remotely by proxy during the coronavirus pandemic. 431 votes were cast with respect to the bill. At the time, no Member objected that a quorum was lacking. Nonetheless, the State of Texas, having accepted the vast majority of the funds that Congress appropriated to it, now contends that the portion of the bill providing protections for pregnant women and workers violates the Quorum Clause.

Texas contends that the Act is invalid because the Quorum Clause required that a majority of Members be physically present on the House floor at the time of the vote. In so doing, Texas asks the courts to graft an additional requirement to the Quorum Clause of the Constitution.

I agree with the majority that the enrolled-bill rule does not bar our review of this particular constitutional challenge. However, I cannot agree with their addition of a new requirement to the Quorum Clause. Even though the majority declares that its reasoning is limited to the question of "whether the Quorum Clause allows proxy presence to be included in the quorum count," ante at 17–18, their conclusion is far more expansive. The conclusion that "[t]he Quorum Clause is concerned with physical presence" shoehorns a much larger requirement into the Constitution. Ante at 28. Because the plain text of Article I, Section 5, Clause 1, historical practice, and evidence of the framers' intent all weigh against the addition of the majority's new "physical presence" requirement, I respectfully dissent.

Judge Haynes did not join the dissent, but a footnote to the opinion reads:

Judge Haynes states that she does not think it is appropriate to throw out the Federal House of Representatives in this arena, so she dissents. She also appreciates Judge Graves's dissent.

Although the majority purports to offer a narrow holding, and only blocks enforcement of the Pregnant Workers Fairness Act in Texas, the opinions rationale would provide a basis for invalidating everything else in the omnibus bill, which included everything from the ban on using TikTok on government devices to the Electoral Count Reform and Presidential Transition Improvement Act.

I doubt this decision will stand. I am not sure the Quorum Clause is justiciable, and I cannot see the Supreme Court upending all of the affected legislation on this basis.

The petition for certiorari in this case writes itself. Another wild card is that the new Attorney General of Texas may not press its case.

More from Derek Muller on Election Law Blog.

#7791. The 2026 Russell Kirk Lecture Featuring Dr. Bradley Birzer

From Heraclitus forward, Western civilization has understood the imagination as one of our highest faculties of knowing. We know through our mind (rationality) and through our stomach (passions), but it’s the chest (the heart or the soul) that bridges both. In his lecture, "Tolkien, Lewis, Kirk, Mythos, and Logos," Dr. Bradley Birzer will examine the ways in which imagination has shaped conservatism and tradition, especially through the key figures of Russell Kirk, C.S. Lewis, and J.R.R. Tolkien.

The namesake of the lecture, famed scholar Russell Kirk (1918–1994), established the philosophical foundations of the modern conservative movement with his landmark books, The Conservative Mind (1953) and The Roots of American Order (1974). He was instrumental in the founding of National Review and Modern Age and was a distinguished fellow of The Heritage Foundation.

Kirk’s political philosophy, summarized in his “six cannons of conservatism,” emphasized tradition and convention, transcendence and piety, political prudence, and ordered liberty. His application of those canons to contemporary issues, through essays, lectures, and newspaper columns, was often provocative and controversial, but always noteworthy. Today, his works and legacy are being preserved and advanced by The Russell Kirk Center for Cultural Renewal. The Russell Kirk Lecture Series recognizes eminent thinkers in the tradition of “the father of American conservatism.”
