#7749. Medieval Settings Are Back In These Mysteries, Thrillers, and Horror Novels

There’s a whole new wave of excellent new genre fiction set in medieval Europe, and since my mother was a medievalist, and I love to mention that fact, I figured I’d do a quick roundup of some new and upcoming releases. Before I get to the recommendations, you may be wondering: what time period exactly are we talking? For the purposes of this article, the medieval era is roughly defined as between 1000-1500, depending on where the characters live. For example: 15th century Italy = Renaissance. 15th century Estonia = Medieval. Burgundy, I suppose, is half and half. Periodization is a continuum much more than a series of hard stops and new beginnings, and the Renaissance is just the Middle Ages with better marketing (see Inventing the Renaissance for more on the debate).

Note: This list is organized in chronological order of setting. Most are new releases from this year or next year, but there are two older titles that are still recent enough to count for this trend. Books that are not yet published have their publication dates next to their publisher info. If you’ve got any Dark Ages-set mysteries to recommend to me, please comment, because I would very much like to read them.

M. T. Anderson, Nicked (Pantheon Books) Setting: Mediterranean Medieval World, 11th Century

This came out in 2024, which I consider recent enough to include as part of this trend piece—especially when considering a medieval time scale. Also it’s awesome. In Nicked, a group of disparate travelers sets off on an odyssey of the medieval world with a common 11th century mission: they’ve been hired to steal the Anatolian relics of a powerful saint and transport them to an Italian city state in hopes of sparking more commerce from pilgrims (the medieval equivalent of taking the Dodgers from Brooklyn to LA). Along the way, they form deep bonds, some blossoming into romance, and take in the sights and sounds of the entire Mediterranean world. M. T. Anderson does that rare feat of capturing the spirit of the time, granting readers a lively, Rabelaisian interpretation of an unfairly maligned era (see history book The Bright Ages for further appreciation).

Paul Brous, The Undying Lamb (Rising Action) Setting: Italian states, 1230

When a book starts with a glossary featuring words from several now-dead languages, you just know that it’s going to be impeccably researched. In Paul Brous’ medieval-set thriller, an Albigensian assassin and an English knight must protect a child with an inconvenient lineage, as a vast array of forces attempt to eliminate their vulnerable charge. Perfect for those who enjoyed Conclave, but wish it had been set waaaay further back in history.

James Bennett, Mother of Night (Evil Twin, March 2027) Setting: Holy Roman Empire, 1291

In this intense work of historical horror, Saladin’s victories have sent a ragged group of crusaders fleeing from the Holy Land, their only option to board a rickety vessel soon enough broken by stormy seas. Shipwrecked and far from home, the few survivors find succor and strangeness amongst a group of miserable swamp-dwellers who warn of danger ahead; the crusaders, determined to forge ahead, do not listen, with predictably dire consequences and a surprising amount of singing.

Ferdia Lennon, Brother Nothing (Holt, June 2027) Setting: France, 1369

Set just a decade before the events of Doom Painting, Brother Nothing follows a newly appointed provost and his precociously intelligent daughter as they flee plague-ridden Paris for a town in the North of France. While their new abode does appear safe from pestilence, other dangers are many, including the perennial threat of English soldiers, an epidemic of children gone missing, and a murder pinned on a prodigal son who confesses to every possible crime— save the crime of which he is accused. As the provost uncovers layer after layer of shocking crimes and terrifying cover-ups, he and his few allies begin to suspect the entire town of conspiracy, for what reads a bit like Red Harvest, medieval style.

A.K. Blakemore, Doom Painting (Scribner, April 2027) Setting: England, 1381

I have complete trust in A.K. Blakemore’s power to render historical fiction as vivid and complex as depictions of the present, and her new novel of the English Peasant’s Revolt does not disappoint. In 1381, England’s most oppressed rose up against the conditions of their serfdom, driven to rebellion by the devastation of the plague and the endless war with France. For 16 days, they challenged the notion that some should rule while others serve, embodied by Wat Tyler’s epic call-to-arms: “When Adam delved and Eve span, who was then a gentleman?” As a side note, I’ve been planning to get a tattoo of that slogan in Ye Olde Englishe font for a while now, so maybe it’s time to bite the bullet. Also the book confirms what I have always known: Wat Tyler had major sex appeal.

Indrek Hargla, The Secret of Saint Olaf’s Church Translated by Adam Cullen (Pushkin Press) Setting: 15th Century Tallinn

Indrek Hargla’s tale of a crime-solving apothecary is based in obscure, and very real, history; the mystery unraveled by the amateur sleuth takes its jumping off point from a mysterious note in Latvian historical records, for a richly detailed and vividly imagined take on a high-water mark in Latvia’s regional influence. In The Secret of Saint Olaf’s Church, the murder of an aging knight leads a city luminary towards a horrifying secret with deep implications for the city’s fragile economic status and unstable power structure.

Indrek Hargla, The Ghost of Rataskaevu Street (Pushkin Press) Setting: Estonia, 1419

Hargla’s second novel to feature apothecary Melchior, released for the first time in the US this month, takes his hero on a dark journey stretching far into the city’s past. When three different townspeople die just after seeing a ghost, the pharmacist and amateur sleuth decides to dig into the matter. In between brewing tinctures, infusing remedies, and proscribing his usual treatments, Melchior keeps circling back to a house in the center of town, once the setting of a terrible crime, and key to understanding the more recent killings.

Jo Harkin, The Pretender Setting: England, Ireland, Burgundy, 15th Century

At the tail end of the Wars of the Roses, an ordinary farm boy is plucked from his simple village life and trained up to become a king. He’s been swapped for a commoner at birth by his dead Earl of a father and forgotten about in the midst of internecine warfare; now, he’s the last hope for the house of York to triumph over its Tudor rivals. But does he have the stuff it takes to fight through his own doubts and become king? And will he survive the endless sacrifices demanded in his ascent to the throne? This is an excellent book to help you understand the inspirations behind Game of Thrones, or the power politics of Elaine’s kingdom in Wheel of Time.

Katherine Arden, The Unicorn Hunter (Del Rey) Setting: Brittany, Late 15th Century

In 15th century Brittany, a noblewoman facing an unwanted union with a far-away lord puts in motion a clever plan to hold off the wedding: her husband-to-be must join her in a unicorn hunt in the dense, dark forest near to her castle. Soon, they find themselves transported into a magical realm beset by an ancient curse that only the lady and her wooing courtiers can break. The Unicorn Hunter takes its inspiration from the real Anne of Brittany, whose marriage to the King of France was just another method of preserving what little sovereignty her province could hold onto under the steady creep of French imperial influence, and who brought two beds to her wedding as a symbol of her independence. I think I would have quite liked Anne of Brittany—Katharine Arden certainly feels a sprightly kinship with the impish aristocrat.

Molly Odintz is the managing editor for CrimeReads and the editor of Austin Noir, now available from Akashic Books. She grew up in Austin and worked as a bookseller before becoming a Very Professional Internet Person. She lives in central Texas with her cat, Fritz Lang.

#7748. There’s a new cozy mystery TV series called The Loch Ness Mysteries

As longtime CrimeReads readers (“CrimeReaders”) know, the editors of this website are always interested in news related to the Loch Ness Monster. Especially me. For example, several years ago, I wrote about how, in 2016, a bunch of Norwegian scientists had sent a high-tech robot down into Loch Ness to scan the, and the robot sent back sonar scans of a creature that looked exactly like the Loch Ness monster, but actually, it turned out to be a model of the Loch Ness Monster built for the 1969 film The Private Life of Sherlock Holmes that had accidentally sunk during filming. So that was a bummer. A HILARIOUS bummer, but a bummer nonetheless.

Any Loch Ness Monster-related news intrigues me. So you can imagine my delight when I came across news of an upcoming series from the BBC and BritBox. It’s called The Loch Ness Mysteries.

It’s set near Loch Ness, obviously, and it’s about a young, irascible, beautiful London detective who winds up being kicked out (I think?) of her job, only to wind up investigating a personal matter near Inverness… and being drawn into a strange mystery near Loch Ness.

So, in the words of the genius who wrote the BBC’s press release, “from Scotland Yard to Scotland Scotland.”

Also, what’s the beautiful, brilliant, difficult detective’s name? DCI Vanessa “Nessie” Keen.

The series will star Melissa George, Jamie Sives, and Ashley Storrie, and will be six episodes long. Ed Sellek of Sister Boniface Mysteries is the creator and head writer.

Filming begins before the end of the year, so stay tuned!

#7746. 8 nonfiction books that delve into the darkest parts of sports

I took up running in 2010. I’d given up smoking and the weight I was steadily gaining was regularly making me cry. My partner at the time had been a serious competitive runner and believed I’d be able to just knock out an eight-minute mile.

In reality, it took me thirteen years and two nervous breakdowns before I finally ran a mile in 7:57, not long after I ran off (not literally) with a vicar. Somewhere in the middle of all that, I’d managed to reach number six in the UK for over-forties women’s tennis. It has gradually dawned on me that sporting success isn’t the healthy, glossy, happybodymaxx endeavour that shiny people on Instagram would have us all believe.

Here are eight books that each reveal a particularly dark but also compelling vision of hot sporting hell.

I read Open when I was on the verge of my own tennis-related nervous breakdown (alas not involving crystal meth like Agassi’s), during a heatwave in Nottingham, in a hotel room full of little flies that I’d become convinced were going to bite me and cause such a severe allergic reaction that I would die. The prologue is one of the best pieces of writing I’ve ever encountered: the extraordinary violence of a five-set tennis match, ending with the wounded competitors lying side by side, holding hands.

Then there’s Agassi’s father’s $10,000 bet (later reduced to $500) that his nine-year-old son could beat Jim Brown, the famous American Football player. The fact that the book was ghostwritten (by the wonderful J. R. Moehringer) gives it an additional layer of weirdness and gothic edge for me.

This is basically an OCD-fest (although officially Nadal does not have this condition) about Rafa being bullied to sporting success by his Uncle Toni. There’s a chilling story about Toni refusing to let seven-year-old Rafa have a replacement bottle of water to teach him a lesson about losing the first one (you don’t need a psychotherapist to make the link with the water bottle shenanigans on court), and another about telling him he must never make himself the center of attention, even when he was the best tennis player in the world.

Even as an adult, Nadal describes extraordinary anxieties, including the belief that if he makes a small mistake, his mother might die. The contrast between the superhuman control Nadal displays on the tennis court and the terrifying lack of control he feels everywhere else is what makes this such a disturbing and compelling memoir.

Serena Williams (with Daniel Paisner), My Life: Queen of the Court

There’s a brilliant scene in the incredible Teddy Perkins episode of Atlanta where Teddy, played by Donald Glover, does a roll-call of famous fathers who have abused their children towards greatness. He mentions Joe Jackson, Tiger Woods’s father and Richard Williams.

Like Andre Agassi’s father, Richard Williams was seemingly determined to create a tennis champion, trying the sport with his older daughters before it finally stuck with his youngest two, Venus and Serena. He would take them to the local tennis courts in Compton with shopping trolleys full of tennis balls. Initially, Venus was the more successful and Serena was determined to beat her own sister so she did not simply become a footnote in Venus’s story.

Swimming Studies was actually the book that set me off on my disastrous tennis adventure. It was a single line in it, something about how Leanne Shapton, recovered from her dark sporting childhood, was still placing in “age-group” events. It was those two words, age-group, that made me think perhaps I could resurrect my childhood tennis dreams.

When I read Swimming Studies, I was myself trying to swim seriously, but ended up with breaststroker’s knee—which is odd, as Shapton suffered exactly the same thing. I felt a little like the book was haunting me, and that I was literally absorbing its ailments quasi-gothically.

Brad Gilbert (with Steve Jamison), Winning Ugly

This was basically my bible during the year I played competitive tennis. Actually, that’s wrong. The Inner Game of Tennis was my bible. This was my grimoire. This may be one of the most fun dark books ever written.

Basically, Brad Gilbert tells you how you can win at tennis (and maybe even life too)—even if you are shit. You do things like turn up early and have a hit on the court with a local coach (impossible when I tried it), then shower, change and arrive late for the match and suggest starting with no warm up. Gilbert has lots of handy hints for ways to deliberately psych out your opponents with chat specifically designed to derail them.

I really loved Finn’s previous book, Running with the Kenyans, which begins with a stirring account of him unexpectedly winning a 5K fun run. After that he goes to Kenya, meets some Big Characters who introduce themselves with their marathon PBs, and becomes himself a more excellent runner. It’s uplifting and inspiring.

But this book about Japanese running methods is far darker. Finn begins this one battling injury and exhaustion and then encounters the weird, workaholic training methods of the Japanese, including running with exaggeratedly short strides and accelerated cadence. There was something bleakly joyless about this book compared with the first one, but I still hoovered it up.

Reading Born to Run isn’t like reading a normal book—it’s an era of your life. My heart skips and I get goosebumps just thinking about it. The ecstatic descriptions of people for whom running is both a way of life and a form of transport, and the theories about primal living, squatting and running barefoot, would go on to underpin my philosophy of sport and life for years to come (and still do).

After reading this book I became a primal forefoot runner. My friend Vybarr Cregan-Reid, author of Footnotes: How Running Makes Us Human, went totally barefoot, despite various broken-glass incidents in British parks. I will never forget the wonderfully compelling romance of Jenn Shelton and Billy “Bonehead” Barnett, and how they would eat pizza and drink Mountain Dew in the middle of their ultras, like running was something even Lana Del Rey could do.

Oh, how I loved this dark and crazy book that made running seem like part religion and part disco-party where everyone successfully hides their pain.

W. Timothy Gallwey, The Inner Game of Tennis

The Inner Game of Tennis changed my entire life and philosophy, and there’s nothing darker than that. I found myself using it as a way of understanding EVERYTHING. The concept is that you have two selves. Self 1 and Self 2. Self 2 will quietly do things if you just leave it alone, but Self 1 is constantly judging. During my disastrous tennis adventure, I could never really get rid of Self 1 and its constant voicings of my coming glory, imminent failure, place in the rankings, what I’d tell my coach, etc.

One of the tricks Gallwey recommends is reading the writing on the tennis ball as it comes towards you. I’ve encountered this kind of method in other places too, like reciting your own phone number backwards during a panic attack.

Another dark sports book I still live by is Steve Peters’s The Chimp Paradox, which has some similar ideas about quieting the crazed ego-animal within. Ultimately, if you can let Self 2 take control, you can enter the mythic space of the Zone or Flow, which is, according to Daniel Kahneman’s incredible book Thinking, Fast and Slow, the most optimal place a human can reach.

Scarlett Thomas was born in London. She is the author of highly acclaimed contemporary cult novels including The End of Mr. Y, which was longlisted for the Orange Broadband Prize for Fiction; Oligarchy; The Seed Collectors; PopCo; The Sleepwalkers; The Runner; and the Worldquake series of middle grade books. Her novels have sold over half a million copies worldwide and been translated into twenty-six languages. Scarlett is professor of creative writing and contemporary fiction at the University of Kent. Find out more at ScarThomas.com.

Major U.S. law firms are giving associates raises and establishing a new market rate ranging from $235,000 for first-year lawyers to $455,000 for senior associates, plus additional bonuses. (Image from Shutterstock)

Major U.S. law firms are giving associates raises and establishing a new market rate ranging from $235,000 for first-year lawyers to $455,000 for senior associates, plus additional bonuses.

Cravath, Swaine & Moore’s associate salary scale was increased Tuesday, and it rivals the raises announced in June at Milbank, according to coverage by Reuters.

Milbank increased the associate salary range from $235,000 to $455,000. In July, it offered special bonuses between $6,000 and $25,000 for associates. Reuters is also reporting pay increases at Fried, Frank, Harris, Shriver & Jacobson and Cleary Gottlieb Steen & Hamilton.

Cravath’s special bonuses—$11,000 to $40,000—based on class year, exceeded Milbank’s scale. Its year-end bonus scale starts at $15,000 and extends to $115,000, which is a continuation of what the firm and others offered in past years.

#7744. Andrey Zvyagintsev on Marriage, Mythology, and the Violence of Family Life

The emotional punch in the gut of Andrey Zvyagintsev’s debut feature, The Return (2003), about an estranged father who takes his two teenage sons on a camping trip, has remained with me, even though I first saw it more than twenty years ago at the Toronto Film Festival. Since then, Zvyagintsev has directed five more films, two of which—Leviathan (2014) and Loveless (2017)—were nominated for Best Foreign Language Film at the Academy Awards. His most recent feature, Minotaur (2026), which is set against the backdrop of mobilization for the war in Ukraine, won the Grand Prix at the Cannes Film Festival.

Based on Claude Chabrol’s The Unfaithful Wife (1969), Minotaur, for the most part, is an intimate family drama. Successful businessman Gleb (Dmitriy Mazurov) suspects his wife Galina (Iris Lebedeva) of having an affair. Their son, Seryozha, is being bullied at school, and the mayor of the fictional Russian city where the film is set, demands that business owners provide him with a list of employees to be conscripted as soldiers—essentially, cannon fodder.

The story unfolds methodically and slowly in the family’s gorgeous home surrounded by trees, on quiet city streets, and in Galina’s lover’s apartment—until it erupts into violence.

Zvyagintsev lives in France and is currently at work on a new film (that I thought was called Jupiter—more details below) about a Russian oligarch. We spoke on Zoom via a translator. The interview has been lightly edited for clarity and length.

A heads up: possible spoilers in the discussion.

Radha Vatsal: I want to start with some general observations: that fathers, wealth or power, and violence, often in the form of unexpected deaths, seem to be a theme that crop up frequently in your films. But there’s also a mythical dimension that we’ve seen in some of the titles like Minotaur and Leviathan, and I’m curious what draws you to this mythical element.

Andrey Zvyagintsev: Only two out of six films have a mythological reference—Leviathan and Minotaur. Only two.

AZ: Jupiter is a name we no longer aim to use because in the Venice Film Festival this year, there was a film named Jupiter. So we could no longer use that name. They did it faster than we could.

[But to answer your question,] Minotaur, the film, has two sides to it. One is a personal family story, and the other is a story about society. So we could say that there are two films inside Minotaur, and they both have a very strong connection to each other. And they are represented in the title “Minotaur.”

Well, the first one, as you know from Greek mythology, is the mythological monster that lives in the labyrinth and demands human sacrifices. And then the other part, the more intimate family side—Balzac has a work called “The Physiology of Marriage” [1829] and the subtitle is “Meditations.” The interesting thing is that Balzac was twenty-five when he wrote that work. He was a very, very young man, and it’s really astonishing that someone so young has such an insight into family and married life.

There is a part where Balzac writes that marital life is like a labyrinth, where the husband wanders in anxiety and watches over his wife. And the husband experiences anxiety when he sees ambiguity, secrets, something unknown in the wife, and he waits anxiously in case there might be a lover around the corner of the labyrinth.

And there is a phrase that Balzac writes, and I’m going to try to quote it to you: That while the husband is wandering around the labyrinth, he’s waiting for the lover to jump out from around the corner; and the lover “minotaurizes”—so making minotaur into a verb—the husband. “Minotaurizes”—that’s the word Balzac uses.

The metaphor is quite simple because for Balzac to give the husband horns, as the minotaur has horns, means to cheat on the husband. But I think it’s also interesting that we do not know what this encounter will entail, and the lover may very well be also the victim of the situation.

So to go back to your question, the title works in two respects and has two sides and explanations to it.

RV: I wanted to discuss the use of interior space in Minotaur. I was very struck by the house. Like the apartment in Elena [Zyvagintsev’s domestic/crime drama from 2011], Gleb and Galina’s home feels like its own character in the film. And there’s a lot of glass and expensive surfaces. It’s also very restrained and tasteful, and it doesn’t match up to the idea we have in the west of new money in Russia being very flashy and in your face.

So I was wondering if you could talk about how you center their home, and also your choice of the décor in their home and the restraint.

AZ: I can tell you that new money—especially the Russians, you can obviously find some crazy mansions and different manifestations of wealth. Much more ostentatious. This house is probably worth $2 to $3 million, which is not a lot of money for a really wealthy Russian businessman.

It was incredibly lucky to encounter a house like this in Riga, in Latvia, where we were shooting, because most houses there have this very European kind of look to them, which is not the style of houses you can find in Russia. And so this house was definitely an exception, and we were lucky to find it.

And in the case of Elena, both Elena’s apartment with Vladimir, her husband, and the apartment where her son Seryozha lives with his family—it was all built for the film. In the case of the house you see in Minotaur, this is a house that belongs to the architect who built it, and he actually lives in it. And the only set that was built for Minotaur is the apartment of Anton, the lover. That’s a studio apartment that was built specifically for the film.

RV: The extended sequence of violence that takes place halfway through the film, without any dialogue, is so engrossing. And I was wondering whether that whole sequence was planned or was some of it improvised? It feels like it takes place in real time.

AZ: It was not improvised at all. It was fully planned beat by beat because every scene that involves blood is automatically very hard to do because you have to wash the blood away after every take and then re-spill it. So it takes a lot of time and effort to do that.

So, as I said, we planned everything well in advance and in a very detailed manner. And we spent five days shooting at the apartment. So day one was love scenes between Galina and her lover. The second day was the encounter between the lover and the husband; and then days three, four, five were all dedicated to the murder scene and the aftermath. So we gave our guy one day to enjoy love, and then the other days, he was getting murdered.

RV: Gleb’s advice to Seryozha when Seryozha tells him that he’s being bullied at school. I expected Glib to be more brutal, and I was surprised that he gave him quite mild advice of how to deal with the bullies.

AZ: You seem to be the only person to think it was mild advice. Where are you from?

AZ:  Russia is a very patriarchal country, and this is how it happens there. The man is the head of the family. And some 100 years ago, children were not even allowed to start eating before the father starts. And if they did, they could be struck with a wooden spoon on their forehead. So this is regarded by many as a normal form of communication between father and children in Russia.

And, this is an important detail: Gleb starts with saying you have to grab [the bully] by the collar, but then he says, do not touch him, but just say with the same expression, tell him very deliberately, if you do something like this one more time… So the advice has two parts to it.

I’m not entirely sure what the tool is against bullying at school and the way children sometimes relate to each other in an angry or violent manner. It’s a difficult conversation. So, it’s hard to tell what the right reaction would be.

This situation is very strange for me. If you have better advice on what to do if a child is getting bullied at school, I would love to hear it because I have a teenage son who is at school in France, in a boarding school, and he also had a problem with bullying, and I also had to give him some advice. My advice was more delicate, but I did explain to him that you have to face the person who tries to bully you and, you know, at least have a conversation.

And going back to your first question about my titles having a mythological connotation, I made a joke earlier about Venice, you know, having a film in competition that was named Jupiter.

But the truth is, I thought to myself that I probably have a few too many mythological titles. So my new film will be called something else, which I cannot tell you right now, but it will be something much better and much more interesting.

RV: Thank you very much. I look forward to seeing it.

Radha Vatsal is the Film/TV Columnist for CrimeReads. She is the author of No. 10 Doyers Street and the Kitty Weeks mysteries, and her essays have appeared in the The New York Times, The Atlantic, the Los Angeles Review of Books, and elsewhere. She holds a Ph.D. in Film History from Duke University. You can find her on Instagram or email: rvatsal@lithub.com

#7742. Wells Fargo faces labor board complaint over union vote

The National Labor Relations Board alleged the lender threatened and retaliated against workers in favor of unionization at a California branch.

The National Labor Relations Board has accused Wells Fargo of illegally threatening and retaliating against employees and coercing workers to prevent fair unionization votes at a California branch.

Most employees of an Atwater, California, branch who signed cards supporting unionization in December 2023 voted against unionization the following month, a regional director of the NLRB alleged, in a complaint filed Feb. 11 and seen by Bloomberg,

The NLRB claims Wells Fargo coerced workers to vote against unionization. Wells Fargo has denied that allegation.

The labor board wants the bank to recognize and negotiate with the union despite the vote, based on a 2023 precedent case. The 2023 Cemex ruling strengthened the NLRB's power to compel companies that violate labor laws to recognize unions.

However, Republicans and business groups oppose the precedent. The acting general counsel of NLRB, William Cowen, or his permanent replacement, could withdraw, amend, or settle the Wells Fargo complaint.

President Donald Trump appointed Cowen acting general counsel this month, days after firing NLRB’s previous chief lawyer Jennifer Abruzzo, a Biden appointee, and Democratic board member Gwynne Wilcox.

The email notifying Wilcox of her termination said she was being fired since she did not “share the objectives” of the present administration. Wilcox’s ouster has left the board with only two members coupled with existing vacancies and does not meet the minimum number of members needed to adjudicate routine cases.

Wilcox is suing Trump, alleging the president surpassed his authority in firing her and requesting that she be allowed to resume her work as an NLRB member.

The NLRB complaint does not signify a complete investigation or a full adjudication of the allegations; rather, the regional office found that the allegations may be sufficient to go to a hearing to consider all evidence and make credibility determinations, a Wells Fargo spokesperson noted.

Employees at the Atwater branch voted 3-1 to reject unionization in January 2024. The branch manager allegedly told staff she knew about organizing discussions and warned about camera surveillance. She also reportedly told workers that Wells Fargo would apply stricter work conditions and would make union supporters stay longer hours.

A Wells Fargo spokesperson said the bank trains its managers to respect the rights of its employees to freely associate and join or support a union, or to bargain collectively with a representative of their choosing.

“We train our managers to comply with labor law and respect the rights of our employees,” the spokesperson told Banking Dive via email. “In this case, the majority of eligible employees freely voted against a union in a Board supervised secret ballot election and the facts do not support allegations to the contrary.”

Wells Fargo is cooperating with the investigation but believes these allegations are unfounded and plans to defend the company and employees, the spokesperson added.

An NLRB hearing before a judge is scheduled for October, and Wells Fargo, if ordered to collectively bargain, can appeal to NLRB members in Washington, Bloomberg reported.

Recently, unionized Wells Fargo employees hit a new challenge in organizing. The bank's conduct management intake team won its union vote 21-16 in December, making it the first non-branch unit at Wells Fargo to unionize.

The team, which handles customer and employee complaints across various locations, has now filed an unfair labor practice charge with the NLRB through Wells Fargo Workers United-CWA. The complaint alleges that the bank illegally refuses to engage in collective bargaining following the certified union vote, American Banker reported. However, the bank contends it’s waiting for the outcome of the NLRB’s review and claims there were procedural flaws in the handling of the vote.

CWA unionized 24 Wells Fargo branches last year, with around 200 employees being organized.

Wells Fargo CEO Charlie Scharf pushed back on employee unionization efforts last April, saying it’s important to “make clear that we continue to believe that our employees are best served by working directly with Wells Fargo and our leadership team.”

#7741. Beyond Lupin: The Brazen Gentlemen Thieves of Fiction

Assane Diop has no use for weapons or threats as he plunders Parisian homes and museums. His meticulously planned heists are executed with a showman’s flair. The anti-hero of the hit Netflix series Lupin, portrayed to perfection by actor Omar Sy, Diop dons elaborate disguises, slips into fake identities, and turns on the charm as he swipes priceless gems and outwits the police.

He models his stylish crimes on the escapades of Arsène Lupin, the top-hatted, monocle-wearing creation of French novelist Maurice Leblanc. Lupin made his debut in 1905, at the height of the glamorous Belle Époque, and was featured in two dozen novels and short story collections. A skilled burglar and a master of disguise, this impish shapeshifter relishes the challenge of stealing the un-stealable and often returns the treasures he pilfers. He’s more interested in righting wrongs than living off ill-gotten gains. So is Diop – he’s determined to exonerate his father, who was wrongly accused of stealing a priceless necklace from the powerful and corrupt businessman Hubert Pellegrini.

Diop’s caper-filled quest for justice made the show one of Netflix’s most successful foreign-made franchises by the time it went on hiatus in the fall of 2023. As Lupin returns for a long-anticipated fourth season, here’s a lineup of five of the slickest gentlemen thieves of fiction:

A.J. Raffles: Lupin was France’s answer to a wildly popular English thief of fiction. In 1898, E. W. Hornung (the brother-in-law of Arthur Conan Doyle) published the first of twenty-six stories on the adventures of Arthur Raffles, a London man-about-town and star cricket player who steals to support his expensive lifestyle and keep up appearances. His speciality is cracking safes and he enlists a sidekick from his school days, Bunny Manders, as a partner-in-crime.

Despite his crooked side-gig, Raffles adheres to a gentlemanly moral code. He shudders at the thought of preying on a host or a friend, and rarely packs a gun when he sets out to steal. “It would be very awkward if anything went wrong,” he tells Manders. “One might use it, and that’s not the game at all.” He stalks the corrupt and the obscenely wealthy, reasoning that “the immorally rich” are the logical targets for a “richly immoral” thief like himself.

Hercule Flambeau: His name may sound like that of a certain Belgian detective, but Flambeau’s obsession is stealing jewels, not solving crimes. That changes after a run-in with a priest and part-time detective dreamed up by writer G.K. Chesterton. In the first Father Brown short story, “The Blue Cross,” published in 1910, the clergyman with a kindly demeanor and a keen sense of human nature foils Flambeau’s attempt to steal a religious relic.

Like Lupin, Flambeau is one of France’s most-wanted criminals – Chesterton described him as a “colossus of crime” with a long record of “ingenious and wholesale robbery.” And like Lupin, he can disguise himself and hide in plain sight, despite being over six feet tall. He is also “a startling acrobat,” wrote his creator, who “could leap like a grasshopper and melt into the tree-tops like a monkey.” Flambeau became a recurring character, appearing in more than a dozen of the fifty-three Father Brown stories, and not only reforms but eventually helps the clergyman to crack cases.

John Robie: It’s the early 1950s on the French Riviera and Robie, a wily burglar whose agility earned him the nickname “Le Chat” before he was caught and imprisoned, is forced out of retirement when a copycat makes him a suspect in new crimes. The protagonist in American travel writer David Dodge’s 1952 novel To Catch a Thief sets out to trap his doppelgänger.

Robie is the consummate gentleman thief – dashing, clever, a master of his calling. Who better to portray him when Alfred Hitchcock brought the story to the big screen in 1955 than the king of suave, Cary Grant. “For what it’s worth,” Grant-as-Robie points out in a line added for the movie, “I never stole from anybody who would go hungry.”

Sir Charles Lytton: Peter Sellers’s hilariously inept Inspector Jacques Clouseau debuted in the 1963 movie The Pink Panther, but the real star of the blockbuster franchise’s first instalment was David Niven. He was cast as the debonaire playboy Sir Charles Lytton, who leads a double life as an elusive jewel thief known as “The Phantom.” Niven was an inspired choice – he played Raffles on screen in 1939, in one of many films to feature Hornung’s character.

The Pink Panther is reputed to be the world’s largest diamond and Lytton has come to a ski resort in the Italian Alps to steal it. The bumbling Clouseau is there to try to stop him. Niven may have enjoyed top billing as a classy crook but Sellers’s over-the-top performance stole the show and hijacked the franchise.

Danny Ocean: Frank Sinatra was the first to tackle the role of the ringleader of a gang of thieves who rob five Las Vegas casinos on New Year’s Eve in the 1960 movie Ocean’s 11. George Clooney revived the character four decades later in 2001’s Ocean’s Eleven, with Danny assembling a team of skilled crooks (an all-star cast that includes Brad Pitt and Matt Damon) to loot a supposedly impregnable Vegas vault.

The movie inspired two sequels, with the gang reuniting to steal a Fabergé egg in Ocean’s Twelve and a casino’s cash and a trove of diamonds in Ocean’s Thirteen. In each movie the targets are fellow thieves or ruthless, unscrupulous moguls. The heists are filled with Lupin-worthy disguises and deceptions and Clooney is a natural for the modern iteration of the cool, classy crook.

It’s little wonder the gentleman thief is a staple of fiction. His victims are fellow travellers who deserve to be cut down to size, or have insurance policies or pockets deep enough to absorb their losses. Admiring their audacity and cheering them on is a guilty pleasure we can all enjoy.

Dean Jobb’s latest true crime book, A Gentleman and a Thief: The Daring Jewel Heists of a Jazz Age Rogue (Algonquin Books and HarperCollins Canada), is a New York Times Editors’ Choice and a national bestseller in Canada. It’s the story of Arthur Barry, who charmed the elite of 1920s New York City while planning and executing some of the most brazen jewel thefts in history. Find him at deanjobb.com.

#7740. The sometimes straightforward, sometimes befuddling certiorari process

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

Each weekday, we present news articles and commentary related to the Supreme Court in a smart, approachable way.

Free readers receive the Friday edition. Full access is for members.

A written companion to Advisory Opinions, bringing together each episode’s key arguments, takeaways, show notes, and source material on the Supreme Court, the Constitution, and the law.

Coverage and analysis of Supreme Court opinion announcements.

Professor Akhil Reed Amar, joined by co-host Andy Lipka, offers weekly in-depth discussions on the most urgent and fascinating constitutional issues of our day.

Divided Argument is an unscheduled, unpredictable Supreme Court podcast hosted by Will Baude and Dan Epps.

One of the Supreme Court’s most critical functions is deciding what cases to decide.

This process has been explained before, but – given the court is now choosing what cases to hear next term – I’d like to use this column to examine some questions about the certiorari or “cert.” process, as it is known. As we shall see, some of these questions have answers; others do not.

First, a review of the basics. The vast majority of cases come to the Supreme Court in the form of petitions for certiorari, a Latin term meaning “to be more fully informed.” The court receives nearly 4,000 petitions each term and grants review to about 60. By a 100-year-old tradition, review is granted when four of the nine justices want to hear a case. When this occurs, the parties file briefs and the justices hear oral argument before issuing their decision.

This process is a blend of transparent argument and secretive deliberation. The transparent portion is that the losing party in a lower court, the petitioner, files a public petition for certiorari, making the best case for why the court should resolve the legal issue in the case. The winner in the lower court, the respondent, also spells out why the court does not need to review the ruling of the lower court. After that, however, the case disappears into the halls and procedures of the high court.

Question one: how does the court handle and process the petitions?

As noted, by 100-year-old custom, it takes four votes for the court to agree to review a case (the “rule of four”). But the vote to grant or deny cert. is not public. We do not know if a petition met with overwhelming consensus that review was necessary or not, or whether it scraped by or just missed out on being granted.

Nor do we know why the court declines to review a case. When the court agrees to decide a case, the final opinion is likely to make clear why the justices were interested. Denials of cert. petitions, however, are not accompanied by any explanation, except in the few instances when an individual justice writes a dissent from the denial of a petition. Justice Sonia Sotomayor, for example, sometimes points out in a dissent or concurrence what she deems to be an important issue of individual rights in criminal cases. But such dissents are relatively infrequent.

This can be frustrating to counsel: Just how much interest an unsuccessful petition attracted would be useful to lawyers trying to decide whether to petition the court in the future on an issue that has been turned down one or more times.

Question two: what roles do the law clerks and justices play?

The answer is known to some extent but secret in other respects. For seven of the nine justices – all but Justices Samuel Alito and Neil Gorsuch – the initial review is by a single law clerk who writes a memo to be shared with the seven justices who participate in a “pool” for reviewing the petitions. Clerks to Alito and Gorsuch handle the petitions on their own.

But much about this aspect of the process remains hidden from public view. Little is known outside the court’s inner circle about how the clerks prepare their memos and what factors influence their recommendation to grant or deny review. The court’s own internal Rule 10 says the court is looking for cert. petitions that either present a conflict in which two or more lower courts have reached differing interpretations of an important issue of federal law, or which, even in the absence of a conflict, present an important question that the court should decide. But those factors alone do not guarantee cert. will be granted.

Just how influential the memo writer’s recommendation is on the judgment of the justices is also unknown. Nor is there any public knowledge of how often justices think the pool memo reached the wrong recommendation.

The cert. pool has been in use by the court for more than 50 years. The justices are certainly able to make adjustments if they find flaws in how it works, and the separate handling of petitions by Alito and Gorsuch provides some check on the process. But since this is largely an internal procedure of the court’s own making, it is not subject to any public accountability.

And the justices rarely discuss it. In his new book, for example, Alito makes no mention of the cert. process or the pool. Ultimately, little is known outside the court about how individual justices handle the pool memos.

Question three: what influences the grant or denial or cert.?

Many factors besides Rule 10 might contribute to whether a petition is granted. Law clerks may be influenced by whether any of the most respected, regular Supreme Court practitioners are involved in the case. Clients certainly think this matters, since they may spend thousands of dollars to hire firms with top Supreme Court practices, those that boast having former solicitors general and former law clerks to the justices as members of the firm.

The clerks may also be swayed by what judges decided the case below, since some of them are especially respected in conservative or liberal circles. In certain instances, a federal appeals court may provide additional fodder to grant review. A party might have asked for rehearing by the full federal appeals court after losing in a three-judge panel. Such an “en banc” ruling, as it is called, can be especially influential, just as a set of opinions dissenting from denial of en banc review also tees up signals about the importance of a case.

Caution also plays a role here. No clerk wants to recommend that cert. be granted only to find that there are procedural flaws in a case (leading to it being “dismissed as improvidently granted”) or that the justices are not inclined to take up an especially ideologically divisive question.

Question four: why are there so few cert. grants?

The number of granted cases in recent years has reached the lowest level in many decades. At the height of the tenure of Chief Justice Warren Burger (1969-1986) in the 1980’s, the justices were deciding around 150 cases each term. Now the number is closer to 60.

There are some possible explanations, to be sure. One obvious factor is the rise of the interim docket, sometimes called the emergency or shadow docket. This docket involves interim requests for relief, where a party to a case asks the Supreme Court to block a lower court order in the interim period while the case is being litigated in a lower court. The Justice Department under President Donald Trump has used this path often, asking the justices to order that a Trump policy be allowed to remain in effect or to take effect after it was blocked by a federal judge.

These interim orders, decided without full briefing and oral argument, are taking up an increasing amount of the court’s time, and some argue that this leaves less time for the justices to add more cert. petitions to be decided on their merits. While this is undoubtedly a factor, the number of cert. petitions being heard by the court each term has been shrinking for a long time, well before the significant uptick in interim docket matters.

Different theories have been proffered by court observers for this decline over time: that Congress is passing fewer new laws that lead to lawsuits and require judicial review; that there is less disagreement between conservative justices and conservative lower court judges, so less need for review; or even that the justices simply like having fewer cases to decide and therefore vote for cert. more sparingly.

It is difficult to prove any one of these theories, and the justices are not providing any answers. In one case last spring involving a state court’s jurisdiction over a products liability lawsuit involving a company based outside the state, counsel for both sides agreed that the court should hear and decide the issue (a rare occurrence, as the winner below typically argues against cert. being granted), but the justices still denied the petition. As is typically the case, there was no explanation.

Question five: when does the court grant cert. before it is requested?

The Supreme Court’s Rule 11 and federal law allow the justices to essentially reach out and grant review to a cert. petition before it has been decided by the appropriate appeals court; that is, before the appellate process has run its course. This once rarely used process has become a much more frequent tool for the justices. Whether they are following the guidance of the rule and focusing on “imperative public importance,” or whether they are impatient to tackle some major legal issues, or whether they simply think it will be more efficient to leapfrog over the court of appeals, the practice is clearly on the rise.

A recent example is Trump v. Slaughter, a fight over the independence of the heads of federal agencies from being fired by the president. The federal government came to the court for an interim stay of the ruling of a federal district court in the District of Columbia that blocked Trump from firing Rebecca Slaughter, a member of the Federal Trade Commission, because there was insufficient cause. The court granted the stay, allowing the firing to take effect, and then also granted cert. and ordered the case to be argued in December 2025.

The process of granting review will continue unabated throughout the current court term. And as it does, questions will continue to arise about how the process works – but one should not hold their breath waiting for all the answers.

Steve Wermiel is a professor of practice at American University Washington College of Law, where he has taught a seminar on the Supreme Court for nearly three decades.

#7739. The top five Watsons (read: “often impressed best friend narrators”) in crime fiction

I don’t mean this literally, I mean this professionally. By “Watson,” I refer to the archetype of the Very Impressed Best Friend And Narrator. A hype man who also tells the story. A deputy who keeps going “wow, look at this guy” as he tells you about this guy. Bonus points if he’s also this guy’s roommate.

That’s what Watson DOES in the Sherlock Holmes series. He’s a carnival barker and a nonfiction writer. Sherlock Holmes is not only his friend, he’s also his subject. Watson isn’t only HIS best friend, he’s also his audience. But he’s also his publicist. He‘s fascinated by Holmes, and he knows tons of people will also be fascinated by Holmes. His job is PR, and man does he do it well.

Assembled for your reading pleasure are five series that follow this general formula: brilliant detective, awed chronicler.

Watson: Archie Goodwin  Detective: Nero Wolfe

In the beloved Rex Stout series, the young Archie Goodwin narrates AND does all the legwork for the affluent, grouchy, high-on-the-horse bibliophile and private detective Nero Wolfe (who hates leaving his luxurious brownstone). Archie, a handsome and dapper young man, is a quick-witted, fast-talking factotum. And he’s always pretty impressed with the mental calculations of his sedentary boss.

Watson: S.S. Van Dine Detective: Philo Vance

S.S. Van Dine takes the Watson gambit even further than Watson does. S.S. Van Dine is a real person, the real-life writer of the Philo Vance books (though “S.S. Van Dine” was a pen name; his real name was Willard Huntington Wright), who writes himself into the stories as the best friend of the brilliant, suave, dandyish detective Philo Vance. Here, he’s not Vance’s creator, merely his chronicler, and the two solve innumerable mysteries together during the Jazz Age.

Watson: Unnamed  Detective: C. Auguste Dupin

We don’t know the name of the guy who narrates his friend and roommate Auguste Dupin’s feats of investigation, but he is really the OG Watson. They meet at various rare booksellers and eventually hit it off, becoming pals and then deciding to move in together. And then the unnamed narrator marvels as Dupin solves crimes, sometimes after hitting the scene of the crime, sometimes without leaving their house.

Watson: Capt. Arthur Hastings  Detective: Hercule Poirot

Hercule Poirot’s best friend Arthur Hastings doesn’t narrate ALL the Poirot stories (he narrates eight of thirty-three novels, and twenty-one of fifty-one short stories), because, after Hastings meets a beautiful music hall performer half his age in Murder on the Links, he marries her and eventually moves with her to South America, where they have four kids. But Hastings still appears, sprinkled throughout the Poirot canon, because he returns to England for business a lot. So they get together and crime-solve then.

Watson: Anthony Horowitz Detective: Daniel Hawthorne

Look, I’d have such a soft spot for Anthony Horowitz even WITHOUT the these books, simply because I grew up reading the Alex Rider series. But the Horowitz and Hawthorne mysteries, in which “Horowitz himself” tags along as the sidekick and narrator (he’s NOT ONLY the Watson, here, but also the Van Dine), are so delightful. I love these guys. Their work is very collaborative (and these books are sneaky, since Hawthorne isn’t the real mastermind, but Horowitz himself). And often, they’re at odds. But that’s fine. This subgenre loves nuance. Horowitz is a Watson with his own (even more impressive) list of mystery bona-fides than his subject, which is what makes this series even more interesting.

Olivia Rutigliano is an Editor at Lit Hub and CrimeReads. Her other work appears in Vanity Fair, Vulture, Lapham's Quarterly, AirMail, the Los Angeles Review of Books, Public Books, The Baffler, Bright Wall/Dark Room, Politics/Letters, The Toast, Truly Adventurous, and elsewhere. She has a PhD from the departments of English/comparative literature and theatre at Columbia University, where she was the Marion E. Ponsford fellow. She hosts the podcasst "Culture Schlock" at Lit Hub Radio. She is on instagram at @oldebean, twitter at @oldrutigliano, and bluesky at @oliviarutigliano.bsky.social.

#7738. The SEC has requested to delay climate rule arguments. What’s next?

Sustainable investing experts are not surprised by the delay and say it is expected to have minimal immediate impact.

Acting Securities and Exchange Commission Chair Mark Uyeda’s decision last week to ask the Eighth Circuit Court of Appeals to delay arguments for the agency’s climate risk disclosure rule did not come as a surprise to regulatory experts in the space.

While the change is expected to have minimal immediate impact, it sets the stage for a shift in focus for the SEC under the Trump administration.

The SEC issued its long-awaited climate-risk disclosure rule last March, nearly two years after it was first proposed — and amid over 24,000 public comments. Uyeda was one of two commissioners to vote against the rule’s approval. The rule was immediately met with multiple lawsuits that were later consolidated into the Eighth Circuit. The spate of legal challenges led the agency to stay the rule’s implementation in April.

Given the agency’s stay and the change in administration, Tom Willman, regulatory lead for artificial intelligence sustainability platform Clarity AI, said Uyeda’s decision came “as no great surprise.”

“It is nevertheless disappointing that investors will be deprived of much-needed financially material information related to climate related risks,” Willman said by email Wednesday.

Julie Gorte, senior vice president of sustainable investing at Impax Asset Management was more blunt in an interview: “The only person on the planet who didn't see this coming was Rip Van Winkle,” she said Wednesday.

Uyeda’s recommended pullback on defending the SEC climate rule follows his prior critiques of the rule. During the hearing on the final climate rule, in the weeks after it was finalized and in his Feb. 11 statement announcing the delay request, Uyeda maintained his belief that the SEC does not have the authority to promulgate the rule or require such disclosures.

Jenner & Block Partner Jennifer Lee, a former assistant director of the SEC Enforcement Division, said Uyeda’s position is “consistent with the new, Republican-led SEC’s shift back to focusing on ‘bread and butter’ investor disclosure issues.” Lee, who now represents companies and financial institutions in regulatory investigations and litigation, told ESG Dive in emailed comments Thursday that she expects that focus to include an emphasis on materiality, while looking to avoid “overly prescriptive disclosure requirements for public companies.”

The change in SEC posture, however, is expected to have a minimal impact for companies or investors, according to Willman and Gorte.

“The impact of this is going to be extraordinarily minimal, partly because it was never enforced in the first place,” Gorte said Wednesday. “So we never had better climate reporting stimulated by U.S. regulatory postures to begin with. And for U.S. companies, or for any company really, a lot of the big ones are probably still going to have to be reporting on all the same things that were in that rule because of [other jurisdictions].”

Willman echoed that note and said that many U.S. companies already voluntarily report climate risks due to investor demand, in addition to growing regulatory requirements both overseas in jurisdictions like the European Union, and stateside in California. New York recently reintroduced its own version of California’s climate disclosure laws.

Additionally, Stephen O’Day, a partner at Smith, Gambrell & Russell, noted the intervenors in the case could continue the rule’s defense, even though the SEC’s announcement indicates this iteration of the agency is not inclined to defend the rules. In the case of the climate rule, 18 states and the District of Columbia have signed on as intervenors to support the agency’s rule.

O’Day said a similar process happened after intervenors continued the defense for enforcement actions taken by the Clinton-era administration for violations of the Clean Air Act by coal-fired plants. Ultimately, the intervenors prevailed, and the Supreme Court upheld the actions.

“The proceedings pending in the Eighth Circuit involve challenges filed by multiple parties and intervenors, any of which could seek to continue defense of the SEC rules,” O’Day said. “So, while the court may grant the requested 45-day pause, it remains to be seen whether any such pause will result in the end of the SEC’s final rules.”

Regardless, sustainability programs and disclosures are expected to continue.

“Regulatory shifts don’t change the fundamental reality: physical climate risk is already priced into markets,” Lukky Ahmed, CEO of climate risk data and analytics platform Climate X, said by email Wednesday. Firms have a fiduciary responsibility to continue to assess, manage and disclose climate risks to their operations, Ahmed said.

“Integrating climate resilience and adaptation strategies isn’t just prudent — it’s essential for maintaining business performance, driving shareholder returns, and protecting communities," Ahmed said.

Despite the shifting federal policy stance, “there is a lot of faith that the drivers of sustainability remain in place no matter who is in anyone's White House,” Gorte told ESG Dive.

“If we don't solve the climate crisis, there are going to be … parts of the globe that are probably uninhabitable, or where people can't work outdoors in the summer. If we don't solve the biodiversity crisis, the prospects are even worse.” Gorte said. “So there are things that we have to do in order to preserve what we think of as life as we know it, and those drivers are going to remain in place.”

#7736. DEI attacks are likely to refine and improve programs, experts say

The intense pressure to end diversity initiatives has led companies to scrutinize their policies. Many of the attacks will end up strengthening DEI programs.

The politicians, provocateurs and think tanks that in the past few years have worked to dismantle diversity, equity and inclusion may not appreciate the full consequences of their efforts.

They’ve used a variety of tactics, in the public and private sectors, including White House executive orders; lawsuits or the threat of lawsuits; shareholder proposals; and needling on social media. They’ve notched high-profile wins, most notably the Supreme Court’s ruling against affirmative action and capitulation at several companies, including retailers and brands that have ended or scaled back their DEI programs.

The successful challenges, inevitably, are forcing scrutiny of DEI practices. But they also provide an opportunity to reinforce DEI goals and execution, which David Glasgow, executive director of New York University’s Meltzer Center for Diversity, Inclusion, and Belonging, sees as a silver lining.

Indeed, the victories are hardly universal. Because diversity, equity and inclusion are good for business for a variety of reasons, most companies are not abandoning DEI. So far in 2025, Target, Nike and Costco are among those that have defended at least some aspects of their policies (in Costco’s case, vociferously). As the Heritage Foundation, a major DEI foe, noted in November, most Fortune 500 companies continue to publicly commit to DEI.

“It is a time for companies to refine and strengthen their inclusion efforts in ways that reduce the risk in the short term — because the risk is real, and we know that — and in ways that are sustainable in the long term,” said Adrienne Pulido, vice president of inclusion insights at Kantar. “So it is looking at both ends of the spectrum, in terms of being very clear about what inclusion means to their business.”

DEI is being pilloried as discriminatory and unfair, yet these systems are designed to create a business that is neither. That is, a business where employees have a variety of backgrounds and perspectives (diversity); hiring, promotion and other actions are executed fairly (equity); and the culture is comfortable and inviting to all who work there (inclusion).

“Unpacking what DEI is and what inclusion is, is part of this moment we're in and part of the conversation that companies need to have about their strategies,” Pulido said by video conference. “What does DEI mean to the business itself? What does it mean to the business and to the future business? Because the demographics of the country are changing, and our research shows that inclusion as a concept, as an idea, is very popular among Americans of all backgrounds.”

DEI goals for most companies are more important than ever because the markets for their products and services are more diverse than they were a decade or more ago, according to Effenus Henderson, who has worked in recruiting, staffing and succession planning at companies in the U.S. and abroad since the 1970s.

“This attack is amplified through the use of social media and technology and psychometrics, where emotions get aroused and reinforced,” he said by phone. “But fundamental to all this is that DEI is not about creating systems that are discriminatory, or about quotas, or a focus on one thing at the exclusion of others. I don't think organizations have really done that. What they have been doing is really trying to expand participation because of the growing demographic change that we're seeing.”

The need to develop DEI strategies that fit with and further business strategies dictates the involvement of leadership, according to Henderson. Too often, though, they are left to the human resources department, leaving companies at risk of adopting DEI programming that is ineffective and possibly indefensible.

“The companies that are able to navigate this generally are the ones where leadership has spent the time talking about it,” he said. “It's not just about reacting to the George Floyd situation or to civil rights laws or litigation. It's really, ‘How do we integrate this as a part of the DNA of who we are as an organization?’ If your organization is more performative, then they don't really understand how it helps to shape business strategy and policy.”

DEI should be treated like any other strategic priority, according to Tim Heneveld, country director for Pergolux in North America. With DEI under the spotlight, it’s a good moment to reassess whether hiring, workplace environment, leadership and operational strategies fit with broader aims.

“That means setting measurable goals, using data to track impact, and holding leadership accountable,” Heneveld said by email. “Some organizations are feeling pressure to scale back DEI, but I think doing so would be shortsighted. Instead, companies should refine their DEI strategies, aligning them with long-term business goals rather than reacting to what they are seeing in the media or any other outside factors. I've experienced, firsthand, workplaces can attract top talent, strengthen their teams, and improve retention.”

In some cases, companies are continuing with their DEI efforts, but changing the names of their initiatives or titles of their employees, experts said.

Crafting DEI initiatives and training is always a work in progress because businesses, markets and demographics evolve, according to Henderson. For many companies, that may mean avoiding those three letters of the alphabet, or the words “diversity, equity and inclusion.” But that, too, requires some thought, he said.

“Is continuing to refer to it under those banners still appropriate, and if I look at renaming it, am I doing that to help enhance our appeal to the markets of the customers and employees we serve? Are we doing it as a reactive, defensive thing for a short-term issue that's hot and heavy right now?” he said. “Get clarity around your objectives, the alignment with your strategies, and then decide whether how you are framing it today will work for you tomorrow and the day after. At some companies, it may mean one thing, and to others it may mean something else.”

The list of lawsuits against DEI programs tracked by the Meltzer Center is long, and getting longer.

Most of these claims invoke civil rights laws intended to end or prevent unfair hiring practices or contracts. Frequently that includes Title VII of the Civil Rights Act, barring discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex and national origin; Section 1981 of the federal code barring discrimination in contracts; and the U.S. Constitution’s equal protection clause, according to Glasgow. The Meltzer Center advises companies to avoid DEI practices that give preference to members of certain groups and involve a tangible benefit.

Evaluating whether a company’s DEI programs run afoul of the latest interpretations of these codes entails enlisting attorneys or other compliance experts.

“This has become a thriving legal practice area,” Glasgow said.

Any business strategy should always be grounded in risk mitigation, and this is just another place for companies to check, according to Henderson. Companies may learn that, to avoid risk, certain aspects of their DEI programs should change.

Others may find that they pass muster. In its proxy statement urging shareholders to vote against a proposal that could have weakened its DEI programs, Costco’s board of directors made clear that the retailer regularly evaluates its “practices concerning compliance with law, including evolving Supreme Court decisions.”

In describing how Costco obeys the law and does not discriminate in hiring, promotion and other practices, the board also provided a litany of protected statuses. This is a reminder that, while civil rights statutes are being leveraged to overturn DEI practices, they nevertheless do bar discrimination for a host of reasons. Moreover, any company that does business abroad will encounter antidiscrimination law that isn’t being disrupted by political activism the way it is in the U.S., Henderson said.

“If you look at Canada, Europe, Asia and South America, there are regulations and laws that support and value diversity,” he said. “So backing away from DEI may, in fact, create harm for your business strategies in other parts of the world. It's not a simple answer, and it just depends on who you are.”

While it may seem like DEI programs are quickly getting scrapped in order to avoid controversy, most are simply under review, Glasgow and others said.

“I think it's prompting a much deeper reflection within companies, not just on what is strictly legal or illegal in what we're doing, but on what has been working and what has not been working,” Glasgow said. “Could we be doing this work more effectively, in a way that actually helps us achieve our business goals, or helps us create the kind of culture that we want to create? Are there things that have been low impact, or maybe even have a negative impact, that we should get rid of, even if it's not for legal reasons? I think the moment that we're living in now could be a helpful reset moment for the field.”

#7735. Kirkland provided $11.8M in free legal work for Trump administration

Kirkland & Ellis has provided at least $11.8 million in free legal services to federal agencies, according to U.S. congressional Democrats in a statement released Thursday. (Image from Shutterstock)

Kirkland & Ellis has provided at least $11.8 million in free legal services to federal agencies, according to U.S. congressional Democrats in a statement released Thursday.

Democrats in the U.S. House of Representatives and the U.S. Senate are increasing their scrutiny of nine major law firms’ agreements with the Trump administration last year to provide nearly $1 billion in free legal services. The agreements allowed the firms to avoid executive orders targeting their legal work, political affiliations and diversity policies.

Kirkland & Ellis performed about $4 million in pro ​bono work for the Commerce Department, as well as $2.2 million for the Defense Department, according to a statement by several Democrats in the Senate and House of Representatives.

The firm also provided free legal services to the Postal Service and the ​International Development Finance Corporation, according to a story by Reuters.

Kirkland & Ellis turned down requests to work on specific projects for the Trump administration, including the renaming of the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts and challenges to the Postal Service’s handling of mail ballots, according to a story by CBS News.

#7734. What is a discriminatory effect? The Montgomery County case and unpacking when schools may try for racial diversity without using race

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.
