#7686. Treating the free exercise of religion and equal protection differently

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

Each weekday, we present news articles and commentary related to the Supreme Court in a smart, approachable way.

Free readers receive the Friday edition. Full access is for members.

A written companion to Advisory Opinions, bringing together each episode’s key arguments, takeaways, show notes, and source material on the Supreme Court, the Constitution, and the law.

Coverage and analysis of Supreme Court opinion announcements.

Professor Akhil Reed Amar, joined by co-host Andy Lipka, offers weekly in-depth discussions on the most urgent and fascinating constitutional issues of our day.

Divided Argument is an unscheduled, unpredictable Supreme Court podcast hosted by Will Baude and Dan Epps.

Two of the most enduring rights in the Constitution are the First Amendment’s protections of the free exercise of religion and the 14th Amendment’s equal protection clause. Should the court’s approach to these rights vary? Specifically, should it be easier to prove discrimination under the free exercise clause than under equal protection?

At the oral argument in St. Mary Catholic Parish v. Roy, on Nov. 3, several of the conservative justices in their questions suggested that a law’s discriminatory effect against a religion should be a basis for striking it down. That is in sharp contrast with a half century of law under equal protection holding that disparate impact (seemingly neutral policies that result in negative effects on a particular group) is not enough to prove discrimination. I would not be surprised to see such “free exercise exceptionalism” from the Roberts court. But it seems to me unjustified.

Colorado, in 2024, adopted a universal preschool program where it will provide funds for children to attend public, secular private, or faith-based preschools. The condition for receiving funds is that the school must consent to “provide eligible children an equal opportunity to enroll and receive preschool services regardless of race, ethnicity, religious affiliation, sexual orientation, gender identity, lack of housing, income level, or disability.”

St. Mary Catholic Parish in Littleton, Colorado, which has a Catholic preschool, and two parents brought a challenge arguing that this restriction on funding violates their free exercise of religion as it requires them to accept students whose families do not adhere to the Catholic Church’s teachings, including LGBTQ children and children with LGBTQ parents. The federal district court and the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 10th Circuit upheld the Colorado law.

The 10th Circuit stressed that the Colorado law did not discriminate on the basis of religion. The court applied the Supreme Court’s 1990 decision in Employment Division v. Smith, which held that the free exercise clause cannot be used to challenge a neutral law of general applicability. This means that the free exercise clause is not a basis for an exception to a law unless it can be shown either that it was motivated by a desire to interfere with religion, that it discriminates against religion, or even that it just creates discretion to treat religions differently from secular actions. The 10th Circuit found that the Colorado law met the requirements for a neutral law of general applicability, as, among other things, it did not treat any one religion differently than others.

The court of appeals also found no discrimination against religious schools in government funding. In 2017’s Trinity Lutheran v. Comer, the court declared unconstitutional a Missouri law that provided public and secular private schools funds for surfacing playgrounds that did not provide the same funds to religious schools. In 2022’s Carson v. Makin, the court applied this to invalidate a Maine law that provided funds to parents to send their children to secular private schools in areas without public schools, but not “sectarian” schools. The 10th Circuit distinguished these cases, explaining that the Colorado law did not exclude religious schools as it allowed them to receive state money on the same terms as all other preschools.

At the oral argument on Nov. 3, there was more focus on the latter issue, perhaps because it would avoid the court needing to decide whether to overrule Employment Division v. Smith. In 2021’s Fulton v. City of Philadelphia, Justice Samuel Alito wrote an opinion concurring in the judgment, joined by Justices Clarence Thomas and Neil Gorsuch, urging the overruling of Smith. Justice Amy Coney Barrett, joined by Justice Brett Kavanaugh, wrote a concurring opinion, expressing support for that view, but finding it unnecessary to decide the issue to resolve that case. The court likely remains divided over whether to overrule Smith and what would replace it.

In the arguments in St. Mary Catholic Parish, there were many questions from the conservative justices that suggested that they saw the Colorado law as discriminatory because of its effects on religious schools. For example, Chief Justice John Roberts asked the attorney for Colorado how this was different from the program in Carson v. Makin and said that the effect of the Maine law was “pretty much the same as the effect of the law here,” as it disadvantaged religious schools. Barrett asked Colorado’s attorney why, if Colorado cannot expressly exclude religious schools from its program, it can nevertheless “impose a condition” – the nondiscrimination requirement – that it knows such “schools will be unable to agree to.”

In other words, these justices suggested that a discriminatory effect of Colorado’s law would be sufficient to find the law violated the free exercise of religion even though the law said nothing about religion and was not motivated by a desire to interfere with religion. The questions suggested that Colorado adopting the non-discrimination requirement knowing that some religious schools would not comply should be sufficient to prove discrimination under the free exercise clause.

Such an approach would be dramatically different from analysis under the equal protection clause. Although I personally think such cases were incorrectly decided, the Supreme Court long has held that proof of a discriminatory effect alone is not sufficient to establish race or sex discrimination. And it has expressly held that discrimination cannot be proven by showing that government officials took an action with knowledge that it would have discriminatory consequences.

Washington v. Davis, decided 50 years ago, was a key case holding that a racially discriminatory effect is not sufficient to establish an equal protection violation. Applicants for the police force in Washington, D.C., were required to take a test, and statistics revealed that Black individuals failed the examination much more often than Whites. The Supreme Court, however, held that proof of a discriminatory impact is insufficient, by itself, to show the existence of a racial classification. Justice Byron White, writing for the majority, said that the court never had held that “a law or other official act, without regard to whether it reflects a racially discriminatory purpose, is unconstitutional solely because it has a racially disproportionate impact.” The court explained that discriminatory impact, “[s]tanding alone, . . . does not trigger the rule that racial classifications are to be subjected to the strictest scrutiny and are justifiable only by the weightiest of considerations.”

The court has even held that discriminatory purpose cannot be proven by showing that government officials adopted a policy with knowledge that it would have a discriminatory effect. Rather, the court has made it clear that showing such a purpose requires proof that the government desired to discriminate. In 1979’s Personnel Administrator of Massachusetts v. Feeney, the court declared: “‘Discriminatory purpose,’ … implies more than intent as volition or intent as awareness of consequences. It implies that the decisionmaker . . . selected or reaffirmed a particular course of action at least in part ‘because of,’ not merely ‘in spite of,’ its adverse effects upon an identifiable group.”

Feeney involved a challenge to a Massachusetts law that gave preference in hiring for state jobs to veterans. At the time of the litigation, more than 98% of the veterans in the state were male, and only 1.8% were female. The result was a substantial discriminatory effect against women in hiring for state jobs. Nonetheless, based on the principles articulated above, the Supreme Court held that there was not a sex classification because the law creating a preference for veterans was facially sex neutral and there was not proof that the state’s purpose in adopting the law was to disadvantage women. The fact that the legislature knew there would be an discriminatory effect against women was thus irrelevant.

There is no way to reconcile this equal protection jurisprudence with the approach several conservative justices suggested in St. Mary Catholic Parish. The question then becomes whether there is any reason to treat discrimination under the free exercise clause differently from under the equal protection clause.

Several justices suggested in their questions at oral argument that Sherbet v. Verner, a 1963 case, justifies concluding that discriminatory impact is alone sufficient for a free exercise violation. That case involved a state having denied unemployment benefits to a woman, a member of the Seventh-day Adventist Church, who quit her job rather than work on her Saturday Sabbath. The court concluded that the denial of benefits imposed a substantial burden on religion; the woman had to choose between an income and her faith. The court thus said that the issue was “whether some compelling state interest enforced in the eligibility provisions of the . . . statute justifies the substantial infringement of appellant’s First Amendment right.” The court found no such compelling interest and ruled that the denial of benefits constituted a violation of the free exercise clause.

Sherbert found a violation of the free exercise of religion based on the impact on her religion despite the law at issue being facially neutral. As a precedent for striking down the Colorado law, however, that is unpersuasive. Sherbert was decided a decade before the Supreme Court held that proof of discriminatory impact was not sufficient for an equal protection violation. And although the court has not overruled Sherbert, it has never explained how it can be reconciled with Employment Division v. Smith. But most importantly, invoking Sherbert begs the crucial question: Should a different standard be used for discrimination under the free exercise clause compared to the equal protection clause?

Conceptually, I cannot understand any reason why discrimination on the basis of religion should be treated dissimilarly from discrimination based on race or sex. Why should two such critical rights be treated differently? Indeed, it is just a doctrinal accident that religious discrimination is litigated under the free exercise clause (or the establishment clause) rather than the equal protection clause.

Applying equal protection principles, the Colorado law does not discriminate against religion in its terms or in its purpose. Many commentators, including me, have argued that – despite court precedent – discriminatory impact should be enough for a claim under equal protection. But there has been no suggestion from the court that it is moving in that direction.

Finally, it is important to stress that even if the law is deemed discriminatory, that does not mean that it is automatically unconstitutional. It means that strict scrutiny should be applied, in which the government action can be upheld if there is a compelling purpose for it. I was disappointed that the conservative justices did not focus on the government’s compelling interest in preventing children from being discriminated against on account of their gender identity or for having LGBTQ parents. Without explicitly saying so, the justices appear poised to carve out a special place for the free exercise clause over that of equal protection.

Erwin Chemerinsky is the Dean and Jesse H. Choper Distinguished Professor of Law, University of California, Berkeley School of Law.

#7685. Not Horsing Around: Carriage owners file lawsuit to challenge new ban in NYC

A recent New York City law banning horse-drawn carriages is unconstitutional, according to a federal lawsuit filed Thursday by a union that represents carriage owners and operators. (Photo from Shutterstock)

A recent New York City law banning horse-drawn carriages is unconstitutional, according to a federal lawsuit filed Thursday by a union that represents carriage owners and operators.

The city council passed the ban Thursday, putting an end to a 168-year industry that has attracted a healthy tourist business. New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani plans to sunset the carriages by June 1, 2028, in all five boroughs in the city. The union representing carriage operators and owners argues that their livelihood has been taken away and seeks to have the ban struck down.

“The city’s approach can be summarized in 12 words: immediately cripple the owners, ignore property interests and contracts, and maybe compensate,” according to the suit.

Additionally, the new law stipulates the “humane disposition” of the horses. Animal rights activists have in the past expressed concern over the welfare of the horses. Earlier this year, an 18-year-old tourist died after jumping from a runaway carriage—the first fatality since the carriages were introduced into Central Park in New York City.

“Our city has changed, and now it is time for our laws to change, too,” Mamdani said.

#7683. Dems ask SEC, DOL to not issue anti-ESG rules: Exclusive

A coalition of 17 blue state finance officials sent a letter to the agencies to counter prior assertions made by their Republican colleagues.

The Democratic finance officials took particular issue with the Republican officials’ letter relying heavily on a federal judge’s ruling against American Airlines in a lawsuit over the management of its retirement plans. The Republican finance officials used U.S. District Court judge Reed O’Connor’s ruling as evidence that the incorporation of factors like ESG is being used to pursue non-pecuniary goals.

The officials included state auditors, treasurers, controllers and comptrollers from New York City, California, Illinois and 12 other states who said that such a characterization of the use of environmental, social and governance factors is “incorrect and dangerously misleading.”

“The decision in Spence v. American Airlines, which dismissed long-term financial interests as a ‘mere pretext,’ fails to reflect the fundamental reality of long-term investing,” the Democratic officials wrote. “Fiduciaries are not speculators — they are stewards of trillions of dollars in assets that must sustain retirees for decades.”

Officials from Connecticut, Colorado, Delaware, Maryland, Massachusetts, Minnesota, Nevada, New Mexico, Oregon, Rhode Island, Vermont and Washington also signed onto the letter. They said that risks related to climate change, governance failures and systemic issues are “present-day financial realities affecting market valuations, insurance costs, supply chains and infrastructure resilience."

The Republican officials had said in their Jan. 28 letter that they held “serious concerns” that funds were being used to advance ESG or DEI goals and asked for rulemaking to prohibit plans from using assets to “advance political or social goals.” They also asked the Labor Department and SEC to issue comprehensive guidance explicitly saying that making investment decisions or proxy votes based on ESG or diversity, equity and inclusion objectives is “inconsistent with fiduciary duties.”

Connecticut State Treasurer Erick Russell called the request a “dangerous political proposal” in emailed comments to ESG Dive Wednesday, while Illinois State Treasurer Michael Frerichs went a step further, calling the approach “Orwellian” and “a reckless attempt to put politics ahead of sound financial decision-making” in comments Wednesday.

“Forbidding investment managers from assessing real-world risks — whether they stem from supply chain disruptions, environmental instability, shifting consumer demand, or any other factor — would restrict their ability to fully analyze investment opportunities and inherently runs counter to that fiduciary responsibility,” Russell said.

The blue state fiduciaries warned that if utilizing ESG factors in investment decisions was banned for fiduciaries, it could cause weaker investment performance, create greater exposure to market volatility and increase financial vulnerability for retirees.

“As stewards of public funds, we have a responsibility to ensure that our investments provide stable, long-term returns over periods of decades,” Delaware State Treasurer Colleen Davis told ESG Dive. “It is morally reprehensible and financially negligent to play politics with the American people’s retirement savings and investments.”

Acting SEC Chair Mark Uyeda and Acting Labor Secretary Vince Micone are currently in charge of two agencies who are defending a pair of ESG-linked regulations in court. Uyeda said last week he would seek a delay in arguments in lawsuits about the SEC’s climate-risk disclosure rule, indicating the agency as constructed is not inclined to defend the rule. A federal judge recently ruled in favor of the Biden administration’s Labor Department on its regulation allowing fiduciaries to consider ESG and other collateral benefits in the case of a tiebreaker. Experts expect that both rules are endangered under this Trump administration.

#7681. Mandatory detention arrives at the Supreme Court – though not all at once

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

Each weekday, we present news articles and commentary related to the Supreme Court in a smart, approachable way.

Free readers receive the Friday edition. Full access is for members.

A written companion to Advisory Opinions, bringing together each episode’s key arguments, takeaways, show notes, and source material on the Supreme Court, the Constitution, and the law.

Coverage and analysis of Supreme Court opinion announcements.

Professor Akhil Reed Amar, joined by co-host Andy Lipka, offers weekly in-depth discussions on the most urgent and fascinating constitutional issues of our day.

Divided Argument is an unscheduled, unpredictable Supreme Court podcast hosted by Will Baude and Dan Epps.

On Oct. 1, the Supreme Court took up a question of considerable importance: whether the Trump administration may continue to detain noncitizens without a bond hearing. This question now sits at the court in two pieces: a statutory question the justices have agreed to answer, and a constitutional one still waiting for the right case. Together, the answers will decide whether people who have lived here for years, even decades, can ask a judge to release them while they fight deportation.

Until July 2025, following passage of the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act in 1996, every administration had detained noncitizens who entered without inspection (that is, without being inspected and admitted by an immigration officer) and were later arrested in the interior of the country under Section 1226(a). According to this provision, ICE may release a detainee on bond subject to an immigration judge’s review (unless Section 1226(c)’s criminal- and terrorism-related provisions apply). In July 2025, Immigration and Customs Enforcement began requiring – for the first time – that anyone who had entered the United States without inspection, whether last year or decades ago, be detained instead under Section 1225(b)(2)(A) for the length of removal proceedings. Unlike Section 1226(a), this provision holds that immigration judges have no power to grant such detainees bond. Two months later, the Board of Immigration Appeals agreed with ICE in Matter of Yajure Hurtado.

Under this policy, the only way one may leave the country before his or her removal proceedings end is discretionary, case-by-case parole, granted only for urgent humanitarian reasons or a significant public benefit. Partly due to this policy, ICE’s overall detained population, which also includes people held on other grounds, hit a reported record of roughly 73,000 in mid-January 2026.

Section 1225(a)(1) deems any noncitizen “present in the United States who has not been admitted [to the country]” to be an “applicant for admission.” The detention command then provides: “in the case of an alien who is an applicant for admission, if the examining immigration officer determines that an alien seeking admission is not clearly and beyond a doubt entitled to be admitted, the alien shall be detained.” The courts of appeals agree that long-term residents who entered the U.S. unlawfully are deemed “applicant[s] for admission.” The dispute is whether that deemed status also means they are “seeking admission,” and would thus fall within Section 1225 and be detainable without bond.

Eleven of the 12 federal circuit courts (all but the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit) have now answered. Nine hold that Section 1226, not Section 1225(b)(2)(A), governs people arrested in the interior: the U.S. Courts of Appeals for the 1st, 2nd, 3rd, 4th, 6th, 7th, 9th, 10th and 11th Circuits. Two read Section 1225(b)(2)(A) as the government does: the U.S. Court of Appeal for the 5th Circuit and the U.S. Court of Appeal for the 8th Circuit.

For the majority of circuits, “seeking admission” is an ordinary phrase Congress left undefined, and as the 1st Circuit put it, “means seeking lawful entry.” A person who crossed the border years ago is not seeking entry; he already entered. The deeming clause in Section 1225(a)(1) may make a long-term resident an applicant for admission, Judge Joshua Kolar wrote for the 7th Circuit, but it does not “conjure a fictional intent to seek admission.” Structure points the same way: in the Laken Riley Act of January 2025, Congress expanded Section 1226(c)’s mandatory detention categories to reach certain unlawful entrants accused or convicted of specified offenses, a needless step if Section 1225 had always reached them. The majority of circuits add that five administrations over three decades read the statute their way, and that Congress would not silently have required detaining some two million people.

For the 5th and 8th Circuits, however, ordinary meaning cuts differently. To apply for something is to seek it, Judge Edith Jones wrote for the 5th Circuit; for example, a college applicant does not stop seeking admission once the application is filed. Several dissenters elsewhere go further and rest on the deeming clause itself, arguing that a legal fiction carries the attributes of the thing it deems. As 11th Circuit Judge Barbara Lagoa wrote in dissent, in a line later adopted by a 1st Circuit dissenter: “If a person whom Congress has deemed an applicant for admission is not seeking admission, it is hard to know what Congress thought it was deeming him to be.”

As for the government’s long contrary practice: “Years of consistent practice,” Jones wrote, “cannot vindicate an interpretation that is inconsistent with a statute’s plain text.” Government-side judges answer the Laken Riley point, too: Section 1226(c) also reaches admitted noncitizens and bars parole, and in January 2025 DHS still treated unlawful entrants as bond-eligible. Both sides now also cite the justices’ own June decision in Mullin v. Al Otro Lado, which read “arrives in the United States” to mean crossing the border, said fears of encouraging illegal entry “cannot defeat the best reading of the text,” and called the rule that every word must do work “not an iron rule.”

The Supreme Court will soon have its say. On Oct. 1, the justices agreed to hear Rhoney v. Barbosa da Cunha, the government’s challenge to a unanimous 2nd Circuit panel ruling for a Brazilian man who has lived here more than 20 years, was detained in 2025 under Section 1225(b)(2)(A), and which that circuit court found to be inapplicable. No argument date is set yet; proposed merits briefing runs into February, pointing to argument in late winter or spring and a decision by term’s end.

But a related constitutional question is also pending at the court. This is whether, even if under Section 1225(b)(2)(A) detainees do not have a statutory right to a bond hearing, they have a right to one under the due process clause. On Oct. 23, the full U.S. Court of Appeals for the 5th Circuit held in the case of Sosnava Rodriguez v. Vergara that noncitizens subject to the government’s mandatory detention policy have no such right.

Judge Cory Wilson wrote for the majority: “Because Petitioners have never been admitted to the United States, due process does not entitle them to additional proceedings beyond what Congress has provided before they may be detained pending removal.” Seven judges dissented. Judge Leslie Southwick countered that the court “has constructed an impenetrable wall between the Constitution and these long-term residents,” who by the record had each lived here for more than a decade.

For now, in Texas, Louisiana, and Mississippi, noncitizens who entered without inspection thus have no ordinary path to a bond hearing; discretionary parole and a few claims the majority reserved remain, but those are narrow exits. The 8th Circuit’s ruling closes the statutory route across its seven states as well.

The 3rd and 6th Circuits, on the other hand, have held that detaining long-present noncitizens under Section 1225(b)(2)(A) without a bond hearing does indeed violate due process. In these circuits, which cover Delaware, New Jersey, Pennsylvania, and the U.S. Virgin Islands (the 3rd Circuit), and Kentucky, Michigan, Ohio, and Tennessee (the 6th Circuit), long-term residents can point to circuit precedent recognizing a due process right to a bond hearing. One’s geographical location thus makes all the difference.

If the court affirms in Rhoney, subject to specific exceptions, noncitizens who entered without inspection and are later arrested in the interior could again ask for bond everywhere, as they could before July 2025. A hearing does not guarantee release, and the burden is generally on the detainee, but the right to ask for bond would be the same in every circuit. If the court reverses in Rhoney, mandatory detention becomes the statutory rule everywhere, yet geography, as noted, would still matter: the 3rd and 6th Circuits have held that a constitutional right to due process requires bond hearings for long-resident detainees like those before them, and the 5th has held it does not.

That is where the case of Putra v. Lopez-Campos comes in. The government’s petition from its loss in the 6th Circuit in that case raises both the statutory and constitutional questions, and the solicitor general urged the justices to take it for that reason. The court only agreed to hear Rhoney, which raises the statutory question, and thus appears to be holding Putra until Rhoney is decided. If the government wins in Rhoney, the split between the 3rd and 6th Circuits, which found a due process right to a bond hearing, and the 5th, which did not, would matter far more, and the justices would likely have to take up Putra to settle the due process issue. But if the detainees win in Rhoney, that constitutional question may never need an answer.

Rhoney should be decided before the term ends next summer. Based on this decision, we will see if the constitutional dispute follows. In the meantime, tens of thousands of people remain detained.

Kemal Hepsen is the managing attorney of Hepsen Law Firm, a federal litigation firm that represents noncitizens nationwide in habeas corpus, mandamus, and Administrative Procedure Act cases.

#7679. Justices to consider disputes over transgender servicemembers, E. Jean Carroll’s jury award, and acting U.S. attorneys at next private conference

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

Each weekday, we present news articles and commentary related to the Supreme Court in a smart, approachable way.

Free readers receive the Friday edition. Full access is for members.

A written companion to Advisory Opinions, bringing together each episode’s key arguments, takeaways, show notes, and source material on the Supreme Court, the Constitution, and the law.

Coverage and analysis of Supreme Court opinion announcements.

Professor Akhil Reed Amar, joined by co-host Andy Lipka, offers weekly in-depth discussions on the most urgent and fascinating constitutional issues of our day.

Divided Argument is an unscheduled, unpredictable Supreme Court podcast hosted by Will Baude and Dan Epps.

The justices of the Supreme Court aren’t scheduled to meet for a private conference – and vote on new petitions for review – for two-and-a-half weeks. But when they do, on Friday, Dec. 4, they will have a number of high-profile cases to consider – which could, in turn, lead to a busy spring.

The federal government and President Donald Trump are at the center of three of the biggest petitions for review up for consideration on Dec. 4.

In United States v. Talbott, the justices will decide whether to review a ruling by a federal appeals court in Washington, D.C., that bars the Trump administration from expelling several transgender servicemembers from the military.

In the government’s petition for review, U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer called the decision by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit “gravely erroneous” and argued that its “reasoning cannot be squared with this Court’s precedents or deference to the military.”

The challengers urged the court to stay out of the dispute, calling the D.C. Circuit’s decision “narrow” and temporary. And in any event, they added, the ruling is correct, because the Trump administration’s ban on transgender servicemembers was motivated by hostility to transgender people rather than “military judgments.”

In another case to be considered, Trump and the federal government have each filed petitions for review in connection with Trump’s challenge to the $83.3 million verdict entered against him in a lawsuit brought by E. Jean Carroll, who had alleged that in 1996 Trump had sexually abused her in a dressing room at a New York department store and that Trump in 2019 had defamed her by calling her a liar.

Trump’s petition for review points to the Supreme Court’s 2024 decision in Trump v. United States, in which it held that presidents generally have broad immunity for their acts while in office. Trump’s private attorney, Robert Giuffra, wrote that “[t]he threat of even a single damages judgment based on official acts will render all Presidents ‘unable to boldly and fearlessly carry out [their] duties for fear that [they] may be next.’”

The federal government’s petition for review asks the Supreme Court to also decide whether the federal government, rather than Trump, should be the defendant in Carroll’s case because Trump made the statements at the center of the dispute as part of his role as president.

And in United States v. Jackson and United States v. Office of the New York State Attorney General, the justices will decide whether to weigh in on the legality of Trump’s appointments of acting U.S. attorneys in Nevada and New York.

Under the Federal Vacancies Reform Act, the federal law that governs how the executive branch can temporarily staff vacant positions that require presidential appointment and confirmation by the Senate, interim officers can serve for 120 days. Under that law, then-Attorney General Pamela Bondi appointed Sigal Chattah as the interim U.S. Attorney for the District of Nevada, effective April 1, 2025, after Jason Frierson, who was nominated by then-President Joe Biden, stepped down.

With only a few days remaining before her interim appointment was set to expire, Chattah resigned, and Bondi designated her as the first assistant U.S. attorney. In that post, Bondi said, Chattah would have the power under the FVRA “to serve as Acting United States Attorney upon a vacancy in that office.” Bondi also gave Chattah the powers of a U.S. attorney for legal proceedings in Nevada.

Bondi followed a similar path for John Sarcone in the Northern District of New York, naming him first as the interim U.S. Attorney and then, when his interim term expired, naming him as the first assistant U.S. attorney and a “special attorney,” effectively designating him as the “Acting U.S. Attorney.”

When challenges to the legitimacy of Chattah’s and Sarcone’s appointments followed, lower courts agreed that neither had been validly appointed. Sauer then came to the Supreme Court, where he told the justices that Chattah’s appointment was not only lawful, but “a critical tool that the Executive Branch has used without meaningful objection for 25 years.” He urged the court to take up that case, and to hold the New York case until the Nevada case is resolved.

In addition to those disputes, the justices will consider three other noteworthy petitions for review on Dec. 4:

One thing to keep in mind: although the justices are slated to vote on these cases for the first time on Dec. 4, they may not act on any of them right away. In particular, for several years, the court has had a general practice of not granting a petition for review until the justices have considered it at two conferences. After the Dec. 4 conference, the justices will meet again on Dec. 11.

Finally, yet another high-profile petition for review is likely to be before the justices soon: Trump v. Clinton, in which Trump is seeking to revive his lawsuit against Hillary Clinton (and several others, including the Democratic National Committee) alleging “a coordinated scheme … to undermine his candidacy and Presidency through fabricated accusations of Russian collusion.” Clinton originally waived her right to file a response to Trump’s petition, but the court called for a response, which she filed on Nov. 13. In her response, Clinton contends that “President Donald Trump and his attorneys” “attempt to frame a routine opinion disposing of a frivolous lawsuit as a threat to ‘the Presidency.’”

Amy Howe is the co-founder of SCOTUSblog and its primary reporter.

#7676. An election impact on the Supreme Court’s immigration docket

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

Each weekday, we present news articles and commentary related to the Supreme Court in a smart, approachable way.

Free readers receive the Friday edition. Full access is for members.

A written companion to Advisory Opinions, bringing together each episode’s key arguments, takeaways, show notes, and source material on the Supreme Court, the Constitution, and the law.

Coverage and analysis of Supreme Court opinion announcements.

Professor Akhil Reed Amar, joined by co-host Andy Lipka, offers weekly in-depth discussions on the most urgent and fascinating constitutional issues of our day.

Divided Argument is an unscheduled, unpredictable Supreme Court podcast hosted by Will Baude and Dan Epps.

The effect of this month’s elections is likely to impact immigration policy over the coming years as politicians and political analysts assess how reactions to the Trump administration’s immigration law enforcement tactics affected voters’ preferences. But the significant shift towards Democrats in states previously controlled by Republicans is likely to impact immigration law even sooner. The Supreme Court is currently considering whether to add to its calendar a case about the constitutionality of an immigration law enacted by Iowa in 2024. The justices had previously signaled their openness to weighing in, but the state’s Republican attorney general, who asked the court to hear the case, lost her reelection bid to a Democrat, casting doubt on the case’s future.

Iowa’s Senate File 2340 criminalizes certain immigration conduct. For example, anyone who has previously been excluded or deported from the United States by federal immigration officials but “is at any time found” in Iowa can be convicted of an aggravated misdemeanor and imprisoned for up to two years. As an alternative to potential conviction, the law allows a state judge overseeing a criminal prosecution to order the defendant to leave the United States. Anyone who fails to leave as required can be convicted of a felony and imprisoned for as much as 10 years.

The state’s law, enacted in April 2024, was designed to closely track federal immigration law. The Immigration and Nationality Act permits criminal prosecution of migrants who are found in the United States after having previously been removed. It also allows immigration judges to order a migrant to depart the United States. By resembling federal law, Senate File 2340’s proponents hoped to assist the federal government’s efforts to penalize and remove from the United States people who had violated federal immigration law.

In two separate lawsuits, challengers questioned the law’s constitutionality. An advocacy group based in Des Moines, the Iowa Migrant Movement for Justice, and two Iowa residents who had previously been removed from the United States filed one lawsuit, while the Justice Department, during President Joe Biden’s tenure, filed the other. In June 2024, the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Iowa sided with the challengers in both cases. Since Senate File 2340 regulates immigration, it treads on an area of law that is the responsibility of the federal government, U.S. District Judge Stephen Locher concluded. As the Supreme Court explained in a 2012 decision, Arizona v. United States, involving Arizona’s attempt to enact its own immigration laws, “The federal power to determine immigration policy is well settled.”

In addition, any time that Congress enacts legislation in an area in which it is authorized to do so, including immigration, the supremacy clause of the U.S. Constitution prioritizes federal law over state law. “Under this principle, Congress has the power to preempt state law,” the Supreme Court explained in Arizona. By enacting a detailed, complicated set of immigration laws, including criminal offenses related to migration, “Congress ‘left no room’ for state regulation” of migration, Locher explained. Since Senate File 2340 attempts to regulate migration, it is likely preempted. Locher thus blocked Iowa from enforcing it.

Within days, Iowa’s attorney general, Republican Brenna Bird, appealed the district court’s decision to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 8th Circuit. While the case was pending before the 8th Circuit, President Trump returned to the White House, and the Justice Department asked the district court to dismiss its lawsuit. Despite the federal government’s shifting position, Senate File 2340 did not fare well before the 8th Circuit. Deciding Bird’s appeal of the case brought by the Iowa Migrant Movement for Justice and the two Iowa residents, the circuit court concluded that each section of Senate File 2340 conflicts with federal immigration law and is therefore likely preempted.

Having lost at the 8th Circuit, Bird asked the Supreme Court to weigh in. Iowa’s law should be allowed to go into effect because it merely “mirrors federal law,” Bird told the justices in her request for review last July. Unsurprisingly, Iowa Migrant Movement for Justice and the two residents who challenged the law urged the justices not to add this case to their calendar. They argued that the 8th Circuit applied the law in line with other federal courts that have grappled with similar disputes, so the court’s intervention is unnecessary.

Last month, the justices signaled that they were more interested in this case, Bird v. Iowa Migrant Movement for Justice, than most others vying for their attention. On Oct. 19, the court invited the solicitor general – the federal government’s top lawyer before the Supreme Court – to explain whether the Trump administration thinks the court should become involved. Calling for the solicitor general’s view is a key sign that the justices are closely considering whether to add the case to their calendar. Of the thousands of cases that the court is asked to review every year, the justices request the solicitor general’s view in a small handful – “around 10 or 11 times every term,” according to SCOTUSblog contributor John Elwood. For that reason, invitations to the solicitor general “serve as powerful signals that a petition has attracted the court’s serious attention,” Elwood explained.

The solicitor general has not yet responded to the court’s invitation, but there is reason to believe it will ask the court to grant Iowa’s request – or would have absent this month’s electoral swing. By voluntarily dismissing its lawsuit last year, the Trump administration removed the federal government from stopping Iowa’s enforcement of Senate File 2340. Since then, it has left no doubt that it stands with Iowa. After the 8th Circuit concluded that Iowa could not enforce the law, the Justice Department urged the full court to rehear the case and side with Iowa. “[T]he panel opinion misapplied preemption principles to affirm the district court’s preliminary injunction,” the Justice Department told the 8th Circuit in an amicus brief that it filed in the Iowa Migrant Movement for Justice’s case.

But the results of this month’s elections may have dimmed the prospects of Supreme Court review. Bird lost her reelection bid to Democrat Nate Willems. Though Willems has not publicly taken a position on Bird’s defense of Senate File 2340, in an interview he accused her of having “filed too many of what I think of as political lawsuits.” He instead said he would focus on “times when there is a real threat to Iowans or a real harm,” and promised to boost the attorney general’s work on behalf of consumers, workers, and the environment. Willems’ Democratic colleague Rob Sand won the state’s gubernatorial election. Sand also has not publicly explained his position on Senate File 2340, but with Democrats holding two of the highest offices in state government, they are likely to align with each other.

Once sworn in as Iowa’s next attorney general, Willems will be able to move forward with or drop Bird’s defense of Senate File 2340. Under the court’s rules, a case will be dismissed when both parties agree. Since Iowa Migrant Movement for Justice and the state’s two residents who challenged the law have indicated that they do not want the court to intervene, all that is left is for Willems to make his view known. Having already lost in two courts, Senate File 2340 remains alive only thanks to Bird’s insistence that those judges misunderstood the state’s role in punishing migrants. But if he wants, Willems can turn the attorney general’s office’s attention to other matters, providing yet another reason why elections matter.

César Cuauhtémoc García Hernández is the author of three books about immigration law and policy.

#7675. After Weil Gotshal’s collapse, law firm merger interest heats up

Consultants Kent Zimmermann of the Zeughauser Group and Jeff Grossman of Oxford Strategic Legal Advisors both said they have seen merger interest increase, with Grossman noting that new candidates emerged after Weil, Gotshal & Manges’ collapse. (Photo from Shutterstock)

The fall of Weil, Gotshal & Manges is pushing law firm leaders to rethink strategy, and many are looking to find merger partners.

According to a Thursday story by Law.com, consultants Kent Zimmermann of the Zeughauser Group and Jeff Grossman of Oxford Strategic Legal Advisors both said they have seen merger interest increase, with Grossman noting that new candidates emerged after Weil Gotshal’s collapse.

“Many conversations were put on hold earlier this year to watch where the economy was going, how AI was going to effect the transformation of law firms,” Grossman told Law.com, adding that interest in mergers “was picking up over the summer, but now the pace is getting faster.”

“A large and growing group of firms want considerably larger balance sheets, greater long-term stability, more money to invest in talent and technology, and other advantages that come with scale,” Zimmermann added.

Lisa Smith of Fairfax Associates offered a slightly different read, telling Law.com that merger demand was already strong in 2026, and Weil Gotshal mainly added urgency for firms that were already considering deals.

“The lesson of Weil is that for firms that are looking to grow and looking to grow via merger or particularly for those starting to see some cracks in the firm, it’s important to go to the merger market while you’re still in a strong position,” Smith said to Law.com.

Smith suggested that firms should approach the merger market from a position of strength. Firms that wait until trouble sets in risk becoming what advisers call a “falling knife,” an unstable partner few want to take on.

“We’ve seen a number of occasions over the last few years where a firm needed to merge with a ‘white knight’ and can only get that when the firm is strong enough to be a desirable acquisition,” Smith said. “For firms that start to see signs that the future is going to be more challenging, it’s important to look at their options early.”

#7674. Jury convicts Palisades Fire arson suspect after retrial

Federal prosecutors blamed a disgruntled Jonathan Rinderknecht for starting a fire near a house in the Pacific Palisades where he had lived with a former partner.

LOS ANGELES (CN) â A federal jury on Friday convicted a former Uber driver on charges he started a brush fire in the early hours of Jan. 1, 2025, that six days later erupted in one of the most devastating wildfires in the history of Los Angeles.

It was the second time Jonathan Rinderknecht, 30, went on trial over his role in the Palisades Fire, a so-called holdover fire from the Lachman Fire heâs accused of igniting shortly after midnight on New Yearâs Day.

At the first trial in June, the jurors split 10-2 in favor of acquitting him, causing U.S. District Judge Anne Hwang to declare aÂ mistrial. The Joe Biden appointee ruled ahead of the first trial that the LA Fire Departmentâs response to the initial fire, and its failure to fully extinguish it, wouldn’t factor in the trial.

The judge scheduled sentencing for March 17. Rinderknecht faces a minimum sentence of 5 years in federal prison and a maximum possible sentence of 40 years, the U.S. attorney’s office in Los Angeles said in a statement.

“We’re disappointed, obviously,” Steven Haney, Rinderknecht’s attorney, said outside the courtroom. “We’re glad the jury gave it its full consideration.”

Haney said they would look into possible grounds to appeal the verdict.

The jury deliberated for two days before finding Rinderknecht guilty on the two counts of arson he was charged with.

Assistant U.S. Attorney Mark Williams said in his closing statement Wednesday that Rinderknecht was angry and mad at everything when he dropped off an Uber passenger just before midnight in the Pacific Palisades, not far from where he had lived in a rented house with a former partner years earlier.

Surveillance camera footage from nearby homes, data from his cellphone and Rinderknechtâs own statements to investigators leave no doubt that he parked his car near a trailhead and hiked up in the dark to the so-called Hidden Buddha clearing in the hills above the houses, the prosecutor said.

A little after midnight, surveillance cameras designed to pick up early signs of wildfires recorded the first signs of a brush fire near the clearing where Rinderknechtâs cellphone data shows he was standing.

âWeâll never know all the reasons why he started the fire,â Williams told the jury, âbut youâve seen some of them.â

Rinderknecht was charged with two counts of arson, one for the Jan. 1 Lachman Fire and one for the Jan. 7 Palisades Fire, which broke out when extreme Santa Ana winds hit Southern California and reignited the embers that had been smoldering among tree roots for six days.

“We’re happy the jury focused on the evidence and came back with the right result,” Williams said after the verdict was returned.

The Palisades FireÂ destroyedÂ thousands of homes in the wealthy enclave above the Pacific Ocean, as well in adjacent Malibu, and killed 12 people before it was contained on Jan. 31, 2025.

Prosecutors claim Rinderknecht was extremely agitated on New Yearâs Eve, citing angry texts he sent to a girlfriend who had told him the night before that she needed space from him, as well as testimony from Uber passengers who rode with him that night and had to endure his rants.

After dropping a passenger off in the Palisades near where he had lived in happier days, the government says he hiked up to the Hidden Buddha clearing and used a large grill lighter that was later found in the glove compartment of his car to set fire to the shrubs.

He then lingered around the clearing as the flames spread and started calling 911 to report the fire â a ploy to create an alibi for himself, Williams told the jury. He also asked ChatGPT if he could be held responsible for a fire started by a cigarette, again to establish a possible alibi, according to the prosecutor.

Investigators took Rinderknecht, who had been identified by his cellphone data and surveillance footage of his car driving through the neighborhood, back to the clearing three weeks after the fire, and he told them that he had gone up there by himself to look at the fireworks but that there werenât any and that he was the only person there.

Haney argued in his closing statement â as he did during the first trial â that there were too many gaps in the governmentâs evidence for the jury to find his client guilty beyond a reasonable doubt.

According to Haney, it couldnât be excluded that the fire was ignited by New Yearâs Eve fireworks because some neighbors had testified they heard fireworks and the surveillance cameras to check for wildfires only create still images with one-minute intervals and may have missed fireworks around the Little Buddha clearing. He also pointed out that the scene of the Lachman Fire wasnât preserved until more than 10 days later and there was no way of knowing what evidence may have been lost.

âThe government has never been able to tell you when the fire started,â Haney told the jurors. âAre you convinced beyond a reasonable doubt that the fire wasnât smoldering earlier from fireworks?â

Assistant U.S. Attorney Danbee Kim said in her rebuttal that the defenseâs argument were mere distractions and speculation, and that Rinderknechtâs own statements to investigators in early 2025 were unambiguous in that he was the only person at the clearing around midnight and that there were no fireworks nearby.

âThese lies are telling â they are not mistakes,â the prosecutor said. âBecause he know that where he was when the fire started was incriminating.â

#7672. Ninth Circuit revives motorcyclist’s concealed carry clash with San Diego sheriff

A federal appeals court gave new life to a Southern California man's lawsuit claiming San Diego County Sheriff Kelly Martinez violated his rights by revoking his license to carry over his membership in the Boozefighters Motorcycle Club.

PASADENA, Calif. (CN) â A Boozefighterâs latest battle in Southern California has little to do with booze or barroom brawls.

Instead, it is a First and Second Amendment fight over whether San Diego County Sheriff Kelly Martinez can revoke Kenneth Shilling’s license to carry concealed weapons because of his association with what she believes is a criminal street gang, the Boozefighters Motorcycle Club.

On Friday, a Ninth Circuit panel revived Shillingâs lawsuit against Martinez, finding a lower court erred in dismissing the action against the sheriff and San Diego County.

Shilling received his license to carry concealed weapons in June 2022 under the previous sheriff. However, his license was revoked by Martinez in December 2023 under a clause in the California penal code requiring âgood moral character."

Writing in a unanimous decision, U.S. Circuit Judge Patrick Bumatay found that Shilling sufficiently claimed his right to free association had been infringed after the sheriff deprived him of his Second Amendment right.

âIn dismissing this claim, the district court misunderstood the nature of the free association right,â Bumatay, a Donald Trump appointee, wrote. âIt asserted that Shilling had to show the revocation of his CCW license somehow prevented him from associating with the Boozefighters Motorcycle Club or participating in the clubâs activities. While preventing an individual from participating in a groupâs lawful activities may be one way to violate the First Amendment right, itâs infringed in âvaried ways.ââ

The three-judge panel found Martinez was acting as a policymaker, rather than a state official, in her revocation of Shillingâs license under the good moral character requirement.

âNo state law mandated this county-specific definition,â Bumatay continued. âIn other words, the county of San Diego â not California â made association with the Boozefighters a basis to revoke a CCW license.â

Bumatay was joined by U.S. Circuit Judge Kenneth Lee, another Trump appointee, and U.S. Circuit Judge Jennifer Sung, a Joe Biden appointee.

“The Bill of Rightâs prevails over politics,” attorney Gary Gorski, representing Shilling, said in an email to Courthouse News.

The good moral character requirement in the stateâs penal code was replaced with more objective and defined criteria in January 2024, shortly after the revocation of Shillingâs license, following the Supreme Courtâs decision in New York State Rifle & Pistol Association v. Bruen.

In his complaint, he described the Boozefighters Motorcycle Club as an organization that is more involved in charitable events than its historical status might suggest. The organization was founded in Los Angeles in 1946 by returning World War II veterans seeking camaraderie over their shared love of motorcycle riding.

The organization says it has never been an outlaw motorcycle gang or part of the â1%â of motorcycle clubs that operate outside mainstream riding activities.

Shilling, a resident of Chula Vista, California, has been a longtime employee at the Chula Vista Elementary School District. He has no criminal history, the panel wrote.

A spokesperson for the county declined to comment.

#7671. Reinsurer TIG found liable over Libby Mine asbestos exposure claims

Omaha-based National Indemnity sued, saying the reinsurer did not fully cover its losses after Montana failed to warn of the dangers in and around the small city of Libby.

OMAHA, Neb. (CN) â An eight-person federal jury found reinsurer TIG liable after Omaha-based National Indemnity claimed TIG didn’t fully cover a sweeping payout for widespread contamination from the Libby Mine asbestos exposure.

Jurors found National Indemnity complied with its obligations under the reinsurance certificate and proved its breach of contract claim against TIG. They awarded National Indemnity $39.2 million in indemnity, $3.2 million in prejudgment interest, $21.1 million in postjudgment interest and $16.1 million in expenses.

They declined to award National Indemnity any future defense costs.

Attorneys for both sides declined to comment after the verdict was read.

National Indemnity Insurance Company turned to TIG Insurance Company and other reinsurers after agreeing in 2022, with Montana, to resolve all coverage claims over asbestos exposure from the mine since the 1960s for $157 million.

National Indemnity insured the state from July 1, 1973, to July 1, 1975; TIG provided the company’s reinsurance at that time.

TIG claimed National Indemnity did not offer adequate evidence and billed amounts not covered by the reinsurance agreement, essentially finagling the numbers to make TIG cover part of the massive bill.

âIt lied," said Scott L. Davis, a Dallas-based attorney for the Spencer Fane firm, representing TIG, speaking of National Indemnity during closing arguments late Thursday afternoon.

National Indemnity said it kept TIG informed throughout the claims process, but the reinsurer never got involved, something it had a right to do.

“They could have helped; they didnât,” Michael Knoerzer, a New York-based attorney for Clyde & Co., representing National Indemnity, told the jury Thursday. âItâs undisputed in this case they never asked.â

In 2004, the state of Montana was found liable for asbestos risk to miners and residents near Libby, a small city in the state’s northwest.

From 1963 to 1990, W.R. Grace & Co. extracted vermiculite at the mine, about 7 miles outside of Libby. Vermiculite, once commonly used for fireproof roofing, insulation and wallpaper, is not dangerous. But the asbestos the mining stirred up was.

Decades of widespread asbestos contamination from the mine caused the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency to declare its first-ever public health emergency during a 2009 Superfund cleanup.

Thousands of W.R. Grace workers, their families and residents since the 1960s have been injured or died from lung disease related to working at or living near the mine.

The fight over who should be held liable started about 2000, shortly after reports of workers falling ill sparked an emergency cleanup. Contamination has since been blamed for hundreds of deaths.

Reinsurance is dubbed âinsurance for insurance companiesâ by the Reinsurance Association of America. Under reinsurance, one insurance company indemnifies another for a loss the company buying the policy cannot handle alone â something that National Indemnity claims TIG did not fully do.

After the $157 million payout, National Indemnity billed its reinsurers more than $101 million. They did not pay. Since first filing the lawsuit in 2022, all other reinsurers except TIG have been dropped from the suit. TIG has paid National Indemnity what it believed it owed â $12.7 million.

According to National Indemnity, the insurance contract required National Indemnity to pay as much as $3 million per loss, with unlimited occurrences. At first, the state said 21 occurrences involved state inspectors not warning miners about the asbestos risk.

But National Indemnity feared that, with potentially thousands of miners and locals affected by asbestos exposure, the number of occurrences could multiply as the matter moved again through Montana courts, with the state Supreme Court telling the parties to litigate the number of occurrences.

Ultimately, National Indemnity and the state settled at 27 occurrences. At $3 million apiece, the bill came to $81 million. The roughly $76 million remaining largely came from past and present defense costs.

Under their contract, TIG was responsible for one-third of National Indemnityâs costs. So, according to National Indemnity, it would have to pay $1 million for each occurrence.

Montana and National Indemnity counted each failure to warn by the state as an occurrence. At issue is whether individual deaths could also count as an occurrence. National Indemnity argued it could have found itself on the hook for âbillionsâ if individual deaths were counted, which led it to settle at 27.

In her instructions to the jury Thursday, U.S. District Judge Susan M. Bazis said National Indemnity would have to prove, by greater weight of evidence, that it performed its obligation under the contract and that TIG breached it, causing damages to the Omaha-based insurer.

The Joe Biden appointee said TIG agreed there was adequate proof of 21 occurrences. National Indemnity would have to prove it provided satisfactory evidence of each occurrence to TIG.

“By greater weight of the evidence” is a less strict standard than the “beyond a reasonable doubt” standard in criminal cases. As in criminal cases, the jury selects a foreperson, and the vote must be unanimous.

#7670. The Supreme Court before it stood apart

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

The Political Supreme Court: A Forgotten History by Rachel A. Shelden (The University of North Carolina Press)

In her excellent new book, The Political Supreme Court: A Forgotten History, professor Rachel Shelden closes with Chief Justice John Roberts’ insistence that “you don’t want the political branches telling you what the law is,” and that public opinion should not guide the court’s decisions.

That will likely sound quite familiar: it is how we have come to think about the Supreme Court. But Shelden’s history shows that the 19th century court and the way Americans perceived it were very different. Indeed, the modern idea of the detached judge, the justice as apolitical “umpire,” is not nearly as originalist as we tend to assume.

Shelden opens with Abraham Lincoln arguing before the court in 1849. The court that Lincoln and his fellow members of the bar knew was not the marble institution, removed from ordinary political life, that we picture today. For example, the justices “rode circuit.” Each was assigned a region, generally the part of the country from which he hailed and in which he traveled through to preside over federal trial courts. This brought the justices into regular contact with local lawyers, officials, and communities.

Shelden calls this “judicial representation”: the idea that a justice would bring a region’s perspective to the court because he knew the people he impliedly represented. Although today’s justices are assigned to a circuit, typically the circuit to which they have ties geographically, the concept is now decidedly different; except at certain prescheduled events, justices no longer directly communicate with the people in that circuit as part of their duties, but handle applications from it in the corridors of the marble palace. “Judicial representation” is most definitely no longer a thing.

But this just scratches the surface of the differences that Shelden lays out. In the 19th century, the justices were active participants in the political debates of their time, in ways that today would not only be grounds for profound criticism but even potential impeachment.

Chief Justice John Marshall was himself an active participant in such discourse. In 1800, before becoming chief, Marshall began contributing to the Washington Federalist, a newspaper established to support President John Adams and later oppose Thomas Jefferson. Marshall’s involvement was so extensive that he became known as the brains behind the paper. Nor did his appointment to the court entirely sever his connection to it. Elias Caldwell, the Supreme Court’s clerk during Marshall’s tenure, subsequently became its proprietor. The paper remained staunchly Federalist under Caldwell’s leadership, regularly attacking the Jefferson administration’s policies as unconstitutional.

Marshall’s political opponents suspected that he continued to exert considerable influence behind the scenes at the Washington Federalist even as chief justice, directing those attacks. Indeed, the Philadelphia Aurora, a newspaper aligned with Jefferson, described Caldwell as “a creature of John Marshall, chief justice.” Shelden casts doubt on Caldwell’s denial of Marshall’s involvement. And given that Caldwell was Marshall’s own clerk at the Supreme Court, you can understand the skepticism.

Justice William Johnson provides another example. In 1823, Johnson ruled (in his lower-court circuit-riding role) that South Carolina’s Negro Seamen Act, which authorized the detention of free Black sailors arriving in Charleston, violated the Constitution. Local officials were furious and refused to publish his opinion in the newspapers. So Johnson took his argument directly to the public, putting his opinion in a pamphlet that was circulated around the country, and then supporting the decision via pseudonymously authored op-eds that submitted his interpretation of the Constitution was correct.

Nor were the justices’ newspaper writings limited to defending their decisions. In 1848, Justice John McLean published letters addressing such political issues as the national bank, taxation, infrastructure, and the Mexican-American War, all while his supporters were encouraging him to pursue the presidency.

And in 1859, Justice John Catron publicly opposed proposed Tennessee legislation that would have enslaved free Black residents who remained in the state. Catron used his connections at the Nashville Union and American to publish a letter criticizing the legislation. The newspaper’s editors attacked his position, producing a public back-and-forth in its pages. Catron’s letter was even reprinted in Missouri, where similar legislation was under consideration. Tennessee ultimately rejected the proposal, and Shelden suggests Catron’s intervention may have mattered.

To put this in perspective, such actions would be akin to Justice Clarence Thomas writing an opinion piece in The Wall Street Journal defending the Republican Party’s position on disputed legislation, or Justice Elena Kagan publishing an article in The New York Times supporting a Democratic president’s legislative agenda.

Yet the justices’ political involvement went well beyond expressing opinions publicly. Some actually ran for elected office while continuing to serve on the court.

Shelden recounts the example of Justice Smith Thompson, who accepted the nomination for governor of New York in 1828 while a justice. Thompson ultimately lost to Martin Van Buren by more than 30,000 votes. After losing the election, Thompson simply continued serving on the court, where he remained for another 15 years.

Justice McLean, meanwhile, was discussed as a potential presidential candidate in the 1830s, with political allies contemplating his nomination even as he continued hearing cases. Indeed, both McLean and his colleague, Justice Levi Woodbury, would later emerge as presidential contenders in 1848.

Justice William Johnson, appointed by President Thomas Jefferson, actually won election as a commissioner of the poor in Charleston Neck, South Carolina, in 1826. In this role, he exercised authority over local taxation, patronage, and public resources. Johnson held this elected position, and won reelection, while continuing to serve on the Supreme Court.

Again, by way of comparison, imagine Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson declaring herself a candidate for the 2028 presidential election – while continuing to decide cases and write opinions. Or contemplate Justice Neil Gorsuch simultaneously holding an elected local government office with taxing authority.

Just as notable was the willingness of justices to involve themselves directly in the work of the other branches of government. In doing so, they corresponded with presidents and members of Congress about public policy. They even offered advice on legislation and, in some instances, helped craft it.

During Reconstruction, Chief Justice Salmon Chase pressed President Andrew Johnson on Black suffrage and used his political relationships to influence Reconstruction policy. For his part, just a few years earlier, Justice John Campbell of Alabama sought to influence President-elect Lincoln to issue a public statement reassuring Southern moderates that his administration would not interfere with slavery in their states. Campbell even offered to publish a letter in his own name, as a citizen of Alabama, to help create an occasion for Lincoln to make such a statement.

When Lincoln declined to act, Campbell turned to President James Buchanan. He urged Buchanan to send commissioners to the secession conventions to persuade the delegates to preserve the Union. Campbell’s efforts ultimately failed. But consider what he was doing: a sitting Supreme Court justice was privately advising both an incoming and an outgoing president about how to address the most consequential political crisis in the nation’s history.

Now imagine Chief Justice John Roberts privately consulting with President Donald Trump about birthright citizenship, or Justice Sonia Sotomayor advising former President Joe Biden about his unconstitutional student loan forgiveness program and how it could be fixed.

In the dénouement of the book, Shelden traces how the political world of the justices changed as the 19th century drew to a close. Circuit riding ended, the legal profession grew more formal, and the court became more centered in Washington. As the country marked the Constitution’s centennial, lawyers and judges helped tell a new story of the court, one that made political detachment seem like some sort of longstanding tradition. (To be fair, this did not bring such political involvement to an immediate end.)

If I have one criticism of Shelden’s otherwise excellent work, it is that she doesn’t explore this transformation in nearly the same depth as she does the earlier history. How, exactly, did the justices (and their fellow Americans) come to accept a view of the court so different from the one they had held for much of the 19th century, and which we hold today? That is a fascinating question in its own right, and perhaps the worthy subject of a follow-up volume.

Regardless, Shelden’s history offers a challenge to today’s justices, as well as to proponents and critics of the modern court. Nineteenth-century justices participated much more freely in political life, while today’s justices insist that they must stand apart from politics, even as many Americans cast a dubious side eye upon that claim. Was it better when justices did not deny the political world they inhabited and were a part of? And can the way we look at the court, and the way the justices see themselves, change again? I don’t think the answers are obvious. But Shelden’s book made clear to me that a reflexive dismissal of such questions is based more on historical ignorance than any fixed tradition of the Supreme Court as appearing apolitical.

Mark Miller directs Environment and Natural Resources litigation at Pacific Legal Foundation

Recommended Citation: Mark Miller, The Supreme Court before it stood apart, SCOTUSblog (Nov. 18, 2026, 10:00 AM), https://www.scotusblog.com/2026/11/the-supreme-court-before-it-stood-apart/

âIâm not directly concerned [by the issues at stake], but Iâm here for my children and my grandchildren,â HÃ©lÃ¨ne Salvat, a woman attending the Paris demonstration, said on Saturday. âEducation â¦ is for our society of tomorrow; itâs degrading more and moreâ¦ I imagine these struggles are a bit everywhere [in Europe].â

âThis shows that weâre at a very particular historical moment, and not only in Europe,â Johanna SimÃ©ant-Germanos, a professor at the Ãcole Normale SupÃ©rieure specialized in the sociology of mobilizations and collective action, said. âYounger generations have known for years now that their futures are going to be dramatically affected by climate change, in a context where their economic futures â aside from the climate issue, which is going to impact the economy anyway â aren’t cheerful either, since the promise that each generation would do a little better than the previous one has been broken.â

Recent events have spurred unions, students and workers to coordinate protests across Europe. Student-led demonstrations in France have fueled calls for education reform, while a resurgence of the yellow vest movement has renewed attention to the cost-of-living crisis.

The October eviction and subsequent death of Maricarmen Abascal, 87, in Madrid sparked outrage over housing rights. Mass protests pressured Spainâs parliament to approve new legislation ahead of an early general election on Nov. 29.

âWe’ve been thinking a lot about how amazing this energy specifically from Spain is, and that the housing movement there has been able to trigger law changes, a snap election, a mass general strike with millions of people in the country,â Samantha James, a member of the London Renters Union, said. âWe want that here, because the government is saying that they’re going to change the way [they do] business, but it’s just business as usual.â

Itâs unclear how the coordinated movement will impact politics and policy.

In France, protests are widely seen as strengthening both ends of the political spectrum, with demonstrators gravitating toward hard-left leader Jean-Luc MÃ©lenchon while far-right leader Marine Le Pen rallies supporters around restoring order and security. In Spain, left-wing Prime Minister Pedro SÃ¡nchez faces an uncertain political future ahead of the Nov. 29 election.

âItâs true that in Spain, thereâs a fear that it will be the far right that emerges victorious from the elections, not necessarily because of these movements, but because it can capture part of the material discontent, yet code it differently politically,â SimÃ©ant-Germanos said. âThat is obviously the case in France; we can clearly see how disgruntled shopkeepers, the idea of disorder, can also benefit the far-right even though this mobilization has led to a very strong return of social issues at the same time.â

#7665. Phumzile Mlambo-Ngcuka, former South Africa deputy president and UN Women chief, dies at 71

South Africa is mourning the death of Phumzile Mlambo-Ngcuka, a trailblazing political leader who served as the country's first woman deputy president and later held a senior United Nations post.

JOHANNESBURG (AP) â Phumzile Mlambo-Ngcuka, South Africa’s first female deputy president and a United Nations under-secretary-general, has died at age 71, the South African government announced Friday.

Mlambo-Ngcuka, a former anti-apartheid activist and lawmaker in the South African Parliament, was deputy president from 2005 until 2008. She also served as minister of minerals and energy and deputy minister of trade and industry. She served as under-secretary-general and executive director of U.N. Women from 2013 to 2021.

The exact date and location of her death were not immediately shared by the government or her political party, the African National Congress.

Mlambo-Ngcuka was part of South Africa’s first democratic Parliament for the ANC after the end of apartheid and white minority rule in 1994 when Nelson Mandela was elected the country’s first democratically elected leader.

Tributes following her death lauded her contribution to South Africa’s struggle for liberation and new democracy and the role she played at the U.N., where she championed women’s rights and gender equality.

âMama Phumzile was a distinguished leader of our movement and a dedicated servant of the people. She made history as the first woman to serve as Deputy President of South Africa,â the ANC said in a statement Friday.

U.N. Secretary-General AntÃ³nio Guterres expressed condolences and called her âa lifelong champion of the rights and empowerment of women and girls.â

âPhumzile Mlambo-Ngcukaâs fight began long before she entered the world stage. As a young teacher in KwaZulu-Natal and an activist against apartheid, she learned that freedom is never complete until it reaches every woman and every girl,â he said in a statement Friday.

U.N. Women said her courage inspired people around the world and her leadership helped shape a global movement.

âFrom her early days as an anti-apartheid activist to becoming South Africaâs first woman Deputy President, and later leading U.N. Women from 2013 to 2021, she devoted her life to justice and equality,â the agency said in a statement.

Mlambo-Ngcuka was appointed deputy president during a volatile era in South African politics and for the ruling ANC, which was experiencing infighting and a bruising succession battle. She replaced former Deputy President Jacob Zuma when he was fired after being implicated in a corruption scandal involving an arms deal.

Despite her known history as a political activist and experienced lawmaker, her appointment drew criticism over her marriage to Bulelani Ngcuka, the country’s lead prosecutor who was pursuing corruption charges against Zuma.

She is survived by her husband and their five children.
